Eastern European dishes.Pierogi: Pierogi are filled dumplings eaten across Poland and Ukraine. Fillings range from potato and cheese to sauerkraut and fruit, and they are common at Christmas Eve.
Eastern European dishes.Borscht: Borscht is a beet soup claimed by Ukraine, and UNESCO added Ukrainian borscht cooking to its urgent safeguarding list in 2022. Many versions are served with sour cream.
Eastern European dishes.Pelmeni: Pelmeni are small Russian meat dumplings that came from Siberia. Hunters stored them frozen outdoors, ready to boil on a long trip.
Eastern European dishes.Blini: Blini are thin Russian pancakes, with a place in Maslenitsa, the week before Lent. Round and golden, they stand for the returning sun.
Eastern European dishes.Kielbasa: Kielbasa is the Polish word for sausage in general. In America the word usually refers to a smoked, garlicky pork link.
Eastern European dishes.Bigos: Bigos is Poland's hunter's stew of sauerkraut, cabbage, and several meats. It is said to taste better reheated over several days.
Eastern European dishes.Chicken Kiev: Chicken Kiev is a breaded cutlet around a core of garlic butter, which spurts out when cut. Its link to Kyiv is uncertain, and it may have been invented abroad.
Eastern European dishes.Beef Stroganoff: Beef Stroganoff, with sour cream and mushrooms, is named for a Russian noble family. It became an international dish in the 20th century.
Eastern European dishes.Kasha: Kasha is cooked buckwheat or other grain porridge. Buckwheat is not wheat at all, but a seed related to rhubarb.
Eastern European dishes.Pączki: Pączki are Polish filled doughnuts eaten on Fat Thursday before Lent. Detroit and Chicago celebrate Pączki Day in the U.S.
Eastern European dishes.Vareniki: Vareniki are Ukrainian dumplings, stuffed with potato, cherries, or cottage cheese. They are boiled, then often topped with sour cream.
Eastern European dishes.Syrniki: Syrniki are fried patties of farmer's cheese, or tvorog, popular in Russia and Ukraine. They are a classic breakfast, served with sour cream or jam.
Eastern European dishes.Solyanka: Solyanka is a thick, sour Russian soup of meats, pickles, olives, and lemon. It is known as a hangover cure.
Eastern European dishes.Paella: Paella comes from Valencia, Spain, so it is not an Eastern European dish. Its saffron-scented rice is cooked in a wide, shallow pan.
Eastern European dishes.Haggis: Haggis is Scotland's national dish, made from sheep offal, oats, and spices. It is honored every January 25 on Burns Night.
Eastern European dishes.Ratatouille: Ratatouille is a stewed vegetable dish from Nice, in Provence, France. The 2007 Pixar film made it famous worldwide.
Eastern European dishes.Moussaka: Moussaka is a baked Greek dish of eggplant and spiced meat with béchamel. The Greek version was shaped by Nikos Tselementes in the 1920s.
Eastern European dishes.Bouillabaisse: Bouillabaisse is a fish stew from Marseille, France. A true one is regulated by a charter naming the local rockfish it must contain.
Eastern European dishes.Risotto: Risotto is Italian, made by stirring short-grain rice in broth until creamy. Arborio and carnaroli rice are the usual choices.
Eastern European dishes.Fish and chips: Fish and chips are the British takeaway classic, and the first fish and chip shops date to the 1860s. During both World Wars, it was never rationed.
Eastern European dishes.Gazpacho: Gazpacho is a chilled Spanish tomato soup, not an Eastern European dish. It comes from Andalusia.
Eastern European dishes.Tagine: Tagine is a North African stew named after its conical clay pot. It is a Moroccan dish, far from Eastern Europe.
Eastern European dishes.Raclette: Raclette is a Swiss cheese melted and scraped over potatoes. The name comes from the French racler, to scrape.
Eastern European dishes.Poutine: Poutine is Canadian, from Quebec, made of fries, cheese curds, and gravy. It appeared in the 1950s and has spread worldwide.

Dishes made with bread.Bruschetta: Grilled bread rubbed with garlic and topped with oil and tomato. The name comes from Italian for 'to roast over coals', so it's pronounced broo-SKET-ta.
Dishes made with bread.French toast: Bread soaked in egg and milk, then fried. It's an old way to rescue stale bread, and the French call it 'pain perdu', meaning lost bread.
Dishes made with bread.Bread pudding: A custardy baked dessert born from thrift: leftover bread soaked in milk, eggs and sugar, a staple of frugal kitchens for centuries.
Dishes made with bread.Panzanella: A Tuscan salad of stale bread, tomato, onion and basil. The bread is soaked so it soaks up the juices rather than staying hard.
Dishes made with bread.Croutons: Bread cubes baked or fried until crisp, usually for soups and salads. The word comes from French 'croûte', meaning crust.
Dishes made with bread.Fattoush: A Levantine salad topped with pieces of fried or toasted pita. The bread is added at the last minute to stay crunchy.
Dishes made with bread.Ribollita: A Tuscan vegetable and bean soup thickened with bread. Its name means 'reboiled', because it tastes best made a day ahead and reheated.
Dishes made with bread.Stuffing: Bread cubes mixed with herbs and broth, a Thanksgiving mainstay. In Britain, the same mixture cooked outside the bird is also called stuffing.
Dishes made with bread.Croque monsieur: A grilled ham and cheese sandwich, often topped with béchamel. Add a fried egg on top and it becomes a croque madame.
Dishes made with bread.Welsh rarebit: Melted cheese sauce, mustard and ale poured over toast. Despite the name, it contains no rabbit, and the odd spelling is centuries old.
Dishes made with bread.Summer pudding: A British dessert where bread lines a bowl and holds soft summer berries. It needs no baking: the fruit juice soaks into the bread and sets it.
Dishes made with bread.Pappa al pomodoro: A thick Tuscan soup of stale bread, tomatoes and olive oil. It's so soft the name literally means 'tomato mush', and it's eaten warm or cold.
Dishes made with bread.Crostini: Small slices of toasted bread with toppings, an Italian starter. The name means 'little crusts', and it's the smaller cousin of bruschetta.
Dishes made with bread.Risotto: It's made from rice, not bread. Arborio rice releases starch as it's stirred, which is what makes the dish creamy.
Dishes made with bread.Polenta: A trap: it's boiled cornmeal, not bread. Before corn arrived from the Americas, Italian polenta was made from other grains such as farro.
Dishes made with bread.Gnocchi: These dumplings are made from potato and flour, so no bread. The name probably comes from the Italian word for a knot in wood.
Dishes made with bread.Paella: A rice dish from Valencia, cooked in a wide shallow pan. The name is the pan's name, and rice, not bread, is the star.
Dishes made with bread.Couscous: Tiny steamed granules of semolina wheat, not bread. Traditionally it is rolled by hand and steamed in a special pot called a couscoussier.
Dishes made with bread.Tabbouleh: It looks like the bread salad fattoush, but it's built on parsley and bulgur wheat, with no bread at all.
Dishes made with bread.Pho: Vietnamese noodle soup with a long-simmered broth. Its noodles are made from rice, so there is no bread in it.
Dishes made with bread.Quiche: A baked egg custard in a pastry crust. Pastry and bread are different doughs, so it doesn't count, though quiche Lorraine is from northeast France.
Dishes made with bread.Lasagne: Layered pasta sheets, not bread. It's among the oldest pasta dishes, and the name may trace back to a Greek word for a cooking pot.
Dishes made with bread.Congee: A rice porridge eaten across Asia for breakfast or comfort. It's cooked from rice and water, with no bread.
Dishes made with bread.Ratatouille: A Provençal stew of summer vegetables such as eggplant and zucchini. It's often served with bread, but isn't made with it.

Animals that might crash your picnic.Ant: A single scout finds your food and leaves a scent trail, and soon the whole colony joins the party.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Seagull: Seagulls learn quickly by watching humans, and they snatch food from people's hands at beaches.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Raccoon: Raccoons have super-sensitive paws, so they can open latches and jars, and they often wash their food.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Black bear: A bear's sense of smell is about seven times better than a bloodhound's, so a picnic basket is easy to find.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Squirrel: Squirrels in parks quickly learn to beg, and they will approach humans for snacks.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Pigeon: Pigeons are descended from wild rock doves, and in cities they treat everything as a ledge on a cliff.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Wasp: Wasps are drawn to sweet drinks and meat, and they can sting repeatedly.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Crow: Crows recognize individual human faces and can hold grudges for years.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Housefly: A housefly tastes with its feet, so it knows your sandwich from the moment it lands.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Monkey: In some tourist spots macaques have learned to snatch food and bags, and they can open zippers.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Magpie: Magpies are intelligent birds that are among the few animals to pass the mirror test.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Chipmunk: Chipmunks stuff their cheeks with food and carry it back to underground burrows, so they can steal quite a lot.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Whale: A whale lives only in the ocean, and could never get to your picnic on land.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Shark: Sharks stay in water and wouldn't be crashing a picnic, though some sharks have existed for over 400 million years.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Starfish: A starfish can regrow lost arms, but it can't leave the sea to visit you.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Clam: Clams live buried in sand or mud and move very slowly, so they're no picnic pests.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Coral: Coral is a colony of tiny animals fixed to the seafloor, which can't move to join you.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are about 95 percent water and can't survive on land.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Goldfish: A goldfish lives in water, so it couldn't wander over to your blanket.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Barnacle: An adult barnacle glues itself to rocks and never moves again.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Manatee: Manatees are gentle sea cows that eat plants underwater, and never leave the water to find a picnic.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Sea urchin: A spiny sea creature that clings to rocks on the seabed and doesn't walk on land.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Narwhal: The narwhal lives in Arctic waters, so you will never find one at your picnic.
Animals that might crash your picnic.Sloth: A sloth is so slow, moving at under a few meters a minute, that it would take ages to reach your picnic, and it stays in the trees.

Cereal grains (from grasses).Wheat: Wheat is the most widely grown cereal in the world, and its gluten proteins are what let bread dough trap gas and rise.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Rice: Rice feeds more than half the world's people, and Asian rice and African rice were each domesticated independently thousands of years ago.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Barley: Barley was used as a unit of measure: an inch was once defined as three barleycorns laid end to end, and it is the main grain for malt.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Oats: Oats were once considered mere horse feed in much of Europe; Samuel Johnson's dictionary mocked them as food for horses in England and for people in Scotland.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Rye: Rye thrives in poor, cold soils where wheat fails, which is why it dominates the dark breads of northern and eastern Europe.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Corn: Corn is a giant grass, and a single ear usually has an even number of rows of kernels, each kernel tied to a silk strand.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Millet: Millet is one of the earliest cultivated grains, drought-tolerant and gluten-free, and it is the main food crop across much of the Sahel.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Sorghum: Sorghum is a drought-hardy grass that is the fifth most important cereal worldwide, and some types are popped like tiny popcorn.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Spelt: Spelt is an ancient wheat relative with a tough husk that protects the grain, and it was a staple in Bronze Age Europe.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Teff: Teff is the tiny grain behind Ethiopian injera; it is so small that about 150 seeds weigh roughly as much as one wheat kernel.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Farro: Farro is the Italian name for ancient wheats like emmer, which Roman legions carried as a ration; it stays pleasantly chewy when cooked.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Quinoa: Quinoa is not a grass at all but a seed from a plant related to spinach and beets, which is why it is called a pseudocereal.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Buckwheat: Buckwheat is unrelated to wheat; it is a seed from a plant in the rhubarb family, so it is gluten-free and a pseudocereal.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Amaranth: Amaranth is a leafy plant, not a grass, and the Aztecs used its seeds in ceremonies until the Spanish banned the practice.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Chia: Chia seeds come from a mint-family plant, not a grass, and they form a gel in water, absorbing many times their own weight.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Lentil: Lentils are legumes, the seeds of a pod-bearing plant, so they sit with peas and beans rather than with grasses like wheat.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Chickpea: Chickpeas are legumes that grow in pods, which means they belong to a different plant family than the grasses that give us cereals.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Flaxseed: Flaxseed comes from the flax plant, the same one that gives linen, and it is not a grass, so it is no cereal.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Sesame: Sesame seeds come from a flowering plant and ripen in pods that burst open, which is the origin of the phrase 'open sesame'.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Sunflower seed: Sunflower seeds are the fruits of a flower head, not a grass, and the head tracks the sun when it is young.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Soybean: Soybeans are legumes, rich in protein and oil, so they are classed with beans rather than with true cereal grasses.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Tapioca: Tapioca is starch extracted from the cassava root, so it is a root product and has no connection to the grass family.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Arrowroot: Arrowroot starch comes from the rhizomes of a tropical plant, not a grass, and it thickens sauces to a clear shine.
Cereal grains (from grasses).Hemp seed: Hemp seed comes from the Cannabis sativa plant, though the culinary seeds have almost none of the psychoactive compound THC.

Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Astronomy: One of the oldest sciences; it predicts eclipses and orbits using physics, unlike astrology, which claims stars shape personalities.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Chemistry: Grew out of alchemy, but dropped the gold-making dream for experiments, and the periodic table now lists 118 known elements.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Geology: Reads Earth's history in rock layers; James Hutton argued in the 1780s that the planet was far older than anyone then imagined.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Meteorology: The word comes from Aristotle's Meteorologica; modern forecasts rely on supercomputers modeling the whole atmosphere.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Paleontology: Studies ancient life through fossils, and has shown that birds are living dinosaurs.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Entomology: The study of insects, the most diverse animals on Earth, with over a million described species and many more yet unnamed.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Seismology: Tracks earthquake waves; their paths bending through the planet revealed that Earth has a liquid outer core.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Botany: Plant science dates back to ancient Greece; Linnaeus's 1700s naming system still lets scientists worldwide name plants the same way.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Ecology: Studies how living things interact with their surroundings; the term was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Genetics: Began with Gregor Mendel counting pea plants in a monastery garden, long before anyone knew what DNA was.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Physics: Explains everything from falling apples to galaxies, and its equations have predicted things, like black holes, before they were seen.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Volcanology: Volcanologists collect gas and lava samples at crater rims, and sometimes predict eruptions from tiny swarms of earthquakes.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Oceanography: Studies the sea; we have mapped the Moon's surface in more detail than much of our own ocean floor.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Astrology: A trap: it assigns personality by birth date, but controlled tests find no predictive power, and the zodiac has even shifted against the actual stars.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Alchemy: A trap: alchemists never turned lead into gold, yet their lab work, including Isaac Newton's, helped lay chemistry's foundations.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Phrenology: A trap: this 1800s craze read character from skull bumps. It was wrong, but did spark the idea that brain areas have functions.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Numerology: A trap: it claims numbers in your name and birthday shape your fate. Number patterns are real, but those links are not.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Palmistry: A trap: palm readers claim creases predict your future, but no study has ever shown a link between hand lines and life events.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Homeopathy: A trap: it dilutes remedies until often no molecule of the original remains, and large reviews find it works no better than placebo.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Graphology: A trap: analyzing handwriting to judge personality has been tested repeatedly and shows no reliable results, though forensic document examination is different.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Iridology: A trap: it claims eye iris patterns reveal disease. When tested, practitioners failed to diagnose conditions beyond chance.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Reflexology: A trap: it says pressing spots on the feet treats organs. It may feel relaxing, but no organ connection has been shown.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Dowsing: A trap: people walk with forked sticks to find water, but in controlled trials dowsers do no better than chance.
Real sciences (not pseudoscience).Crystal healing: A trap: the belief that stones channel healing energy has no scientific support; any benefit seems to be placebo.

Films where animals talk.Babe: The 1995 film about a pig who herds sheep mixed real animals with animatronics, and was nominated for Best Picture.
Films where animals talk.Zootopia: Disney's 2016 city of mammals; designers made districts to every species' scale, from tiny rodent streets to giraffe-high ones.
Films where animals talk.The Lion King: Loosely inspired by Hamlet, the 1994 film became the highest-grossing hand-drawn animated film ever.
Films where animals talk.Madagascar: The film's lemurs are real animals found nowhere in the wild but the island of Madagascar.
Films where animals talk.Dr. Dolittle: Hugh Lofting's doctor learned animal languages from his parrot, Polynesia, in books begun in World War I trenches.
Films where animals talk.Stuart Little: E. B. White's mouse, who rides in a mouse-sized car, inspired the film where the mouse is a computer-animated star.
Films where animals talk.Charlotte's Web: E. B. White wrote it after watching a real barn spider in his Maine barn spin an egg sac.
Films where animals talk.Bolt: A TV-star dog who thinks his show's superpowers are real. The cat Mittens talks to him, while humans hear only meows.
Films where animals talk.Kung Fu Panda: The 2008 film's heroes each embody a real martial arts style, such as Tigress with tiger-style kung fu.
Films where animals talk.Ratatouille: Pixar consulted chef Thomas Keller, whose own version of the title dish appears at the film's climax.
Films where animals talk.Paddington: Michael Bond's bear came from Darkest Peru and keeps an emergency marmalade sandwich under his hat.
Films where animals talk.Fantastic Mr. Fox: Wes Anderson's 2009 stop-motion version of Roald Dahl's book; the cast reportedly recorded outdoors, in barns and mud, instead of booths.
Films where animals talk.Chicken Run: Aardman's 1999 film about hens escaping a farm is one of the highest-grossing stop-motion films ever.
Films where animals talk.Finding Nemo: Real clownfish are born male and the dominant one turns female if the female dies, so Marlin would actually become a mother.
Films where animals talk.Free Willy: Willy the orca never speaks. The real orca who played him, Keiko, was later returned toward Icelandic waters.
Films where animals talk.Jaws: The shark never speaks. The mechanical shark, nicknamed Bruce, broke down so often that Spielberg had to show it sparingly.
Films where animals talk.Marley & Me: The dog narrated through a memoir, not speech. John Grogan's book became a bestseller about his chaotic Labrador.
Films where animals talk.Hachi: Hachi: A Dog's Tale (2009) retells the real Akita Hachiko, who waited years at Tokyo's Shibuya station for his dead owner.
Films where animals talk.Lassie: Lassie, a female character, was played by male collies, which are larger and keep fuller coats.
Films where animals talk.Old Yeller: The 1957 Disney tearjerker about a yellow stray dog, who communicates only by barking.
Films where animals talk.Seabiscuit: The 1930s underdog racehorse beat the champion War Admiral in 1938, a real-life story needing no talking.
Films where animals talk.War Horse: Michael Morpurgo's story became a stage play with life-size horse puppets, but no animal speaks in it.
Films where animals talk.King Kong: Kong roars but never talks. The 1933 original used stop-motion models only about eighteen inches tall.
Films where animals talk.Godzilla: The monster's roar was made by rubbing a resin-coated glove along a double bass string, but he doesn't talk.

Brass instruments.Trumpet: Its modern three-valve design came in the early 1800s, and Louis Armstrong and Miles Davis are among its jazz legends.
Brass instruments.Trombone: The slide lets players change pitch continuously, and the instrument's name literally means 'big trumpet' in Italian.
Brass instruments.Tuba: The largest brass instrument holds around 18 feet of tubing wound into a coil, and gives the orchestra its lowest notes.
Brass instruments.French horn: The 'French' horn isn't French but German in origin, and its coiled tube is about 12 feet long.
Brass instruments.Cornet: A cornet looks like a short trumpet, but its conical bore gives a mellower sound, and it is the lead in British brass bands.
Brass instruments.Flugelhorn: This mellow, fat-sounding relative of the trumpet is a jazz favorite, and was used by Chuck Mangione on his hit Feels So Good.
Brass instruments.Euphonium: Its name comes from the Greek for 'sweet-voiced', and it is the tenor voice of brass bands.
Brass instruments.Bugle: With no valves, it plays only notes of the overtone series, which is why military calls like Taps use only a few pitches.
Brass instruments.Sousaphone: Named after composer John Philip Sousa, this marching tuba wraps around the player's body so it can be carried while moving.
Brass instruments.Saxophone: Despite its metal body, it is a woodwind, as it uses a single reed. Adolphe Sax invented it in the 1840s.
Brass instruments.Flute: A modern flute is usually metal, but is a woodwind, since sound comes from air across a hole, not buzzing lips.
Brass instruments.Clarinet: A woodwind, since its sound comes from a vibrating reed rather than lips buzzing into a mouthpiece.
Brass instruments.Oboe: A double-reed woodwind. Brass requires the player's lips to buzz, but the oboe doesn't.
Brass instruments.Bassoon: A double-reed woodwind with about 9 feet of folded tubing and a deep, reedy voice, so it fits the woodwinds and not brass.
Brass instruments.Piccolo: A tiny flute, a woodwind, that sounds an octave higher than the standard flute, and is often played in marching bands.
Brass instruments.Harmonica: Players blow and draw air across metal reeds, a free-reed wind instrument. It has metal parts, but it's not brass.
Brass instruments.Recorder: A simple whistle-like flute, mostly of wood or plastic, found in schools, it is a woodwind with no buzzing lips.
Brass instruments.Bagpipes: A reed instrument fed by air from a bag, often played in Scotland. Players do not buzz their lips as brass players do.
Brass instruments.Cello: A bowed string instrument, whose sound comes from vibrating strings and not from buzzing lips in a metal tube.
Brass instruments.Triangle: A bent steel bar that is struck, so it is a percussion instrument, even though it's metal like a brass one.
Brass instruments.Cymbal: Cymbals are percussion, and though they're often made of bronze or brass alloy, they're not a brass instrument.
Brass instruments.Kazoo: It is a humming toy with a vibrating membrane, so it has nothing to do with the brass family.
Brass instruments.Ocarina: A small ceramic wind instrument, played by blowing across a hole, so the clay body keeps it out of brass.
Brass instruments.Accordion: A free-reed instrument with bellows, which squeezes air over reeds, so it's not brass despite its shiny keys.

Italian composers.Vivaldi: Venetian priest and violinist whose Four Seasons is one of the most recorded works in classical music.
Italian composers.Verdi: Italy's operatic giant. At Verdi's 1901 funeral, an estimated 200,000 people lined the streets of Milan.
Italian composers.Puccini: He died in 1924 with Turandot unfinished, and at its premiere the conductor stopped where the composer's work ended.
Italian composers.Rossini: He wrote The Barber of Seville in a few weeks, then retired from opera at 37 to cook. A steak dish bears his name.
Italian composers.Monteverdi: His 1607 Orfeo is among the earliest operas still regularly staged, nearly 400 years later.
Italian composers.Paganini: A violin virtuoso so dazzling that rumor claimed he had sold his soul to the devil.
Italian composers.Corelli: A Baroque violinist-composer from Fusignano whose music helped shape the concerto.
Italian composers.Scarlatti: Domenico wrote 555 keyboard sonatas, mostly while serving the Spanish and Portuguese courts.
Italian composers.Donizetti: He wrote about 70 operas, including Lucia di Lammermoor and the comic L'elisir d'amore.
Italian composers.Bellini: A master of long, floating melodies, he wrote Norma and died at only 33.
Italian composers.Morricone: The film composer behind The Good, the Bad and the Ugly won an honorary Oscar in 2007 and a regular one in 2016.
Italian composers.Mozart: Austrian, born in Salzburg, though he wrote Italian operas such as The Marriage of Figaro and Don Giovanni.
Italian composers.Chopin: Polish, not Italian. He wrote almost entirely for piano and spent his adult life in Paris.
Italian composers.Bizet: French, not Italian. His Carmen flopped at its 1875 premiere, and he died just months later aged 36.
Italian composers.Debussy: French Impressionist whose pieces are often described in terms of painting rather than classical form.
Italian composers.Wagner: German, born in Leipzig, so not Italian, though he died in Venice in 1883 and wrote his last works there.
Italian composers.Handel: German-born but he studied in Italy and made his name there, which is why he's a tempting trap. He later became British.
Italian composers.Strauss: Johann Strauss II was Viennese, the Waltz King, so Austrian rather than Italian.
Italian composers.Liszt: Hungarian, though he took minor orders in Rome and lived in Italy for years.
Italian composers.Gounod: French, and best known for the opera Faust and an Ave Maria set over a Bach prelude.
Italian composers.Offenbach: German-born, French-based, king of the operetta, with a can-can in Orpheus in the Underworld.
Italian composers.Grieg: Norwegian, so not Italian. His Peer Gynt suite, with In the Hall of the Mountain King, was written for Ibsen's play.
Italian composers.Ravel: French, not Italian, though his Boléro is often performed with Spanish flavor, since his mother was Basque.
Italian composers.Satie: French eccentric whose Gymnopédies are quiet and repetitive, which some call proto-ambient music.

Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Spoon: Spoons are far older than forks, which only became common at European dinner tables within the last few centuries.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.June: June is thought to be named for Juno, the Roman goddess of marriage, which may explain its popularity for weddings.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Noon: Noon began as the Latin 'ninth hour', about 3 pm, and slid back to midday over the Middle Ages.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Balloon: The first crewed flight in a hot-air balloon took place in Paris in 1783, built by the Montgolfier brothers.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Cartoon: A cartoon originally meant a full-size preparatory drawing for a painting or tapestry, long before comics.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Raccoon: The raccoon's scientific name, Procyon lotor, means roughly 'washer', for the way it dunks and rubs its food.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Lagoon: Atoll lagoons form where coral rings a sinking volcano, an idea Charles Darwin worked out in the 1830s.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Baboon: Baboons are among the largest monkeys, living in troops of dozens, sometimes over a hundred.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Dune: Some dunes 'boom' or 'sing' when sand avalanches down their slip face, a hum heard across desert valleys.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Prune: Prune also means to cut back branches, and a late-winter pruning can make a rose bloom more strongly.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Monsoon: Monsoon comes from the Arabic word mawsim, meaning 'season', and it names a seasonal wind reversal, not just heavy rain.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Bassoon: The bassoon is about 2.5 metres of tubing folded into a body you can hold, and it's sounded with a double reed.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Tone: Tone rhymes with bone. The vowel is a long o, nothing like tune's oo.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Tin: Tin rhymes with win, so only the t at the start matches tune.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Ton: Ton rhymes with sun, a near miss that fools many, since the short u makes it nothing like tune.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Town: Town rhymes with down; its ow vowel is wrong for tune, though both end in n.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Torn: Torn rhymes with born, and its r-colored vowel doesn't match tune's.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Lemon: Lemon has no true rhyme in English, so it's a trap even though it ends in an n sound.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Salmon: The l in salmon is silent (SAM-un), and it ends in a soft -un, not -oon.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Moan: Moan rhymes with bone and tone; the long o is the wrong vowel for tune.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Bone: Bone rhymes with tone and moan, and the long o is the opposite of tune's oo.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Gown: Gown rhymes with down and town, and its ow sound isn't tune's.
Words that rhyme with 'tune'.Room: Room has the oo vowel but ends in m, so it rhymes with doom, not tune.

Words that go before 'note'.Bank: A banknote is paper currency. England's earliest notes, from the 1690s, were handwritten promises from the Bank of England.
Words that go before 'note'.Foot: A footnote sits at the bottom of a page. Some scholarly books have more footnote text than main text.
Words that go before 'note'.Sticky: The Post-it, invented at 3M, came from a weak glue failure by Spencer Silver. Art Fry used it to mark his hymnbook.
Words that go before 'note'.Sick: A sick note is a doctor's or parent's excuse for missing work or school. In the UK, it's now often called a fit note.
Words that go before 'note'.Love: A love note can be a few words on a napkin. Notes like these are among the oldest forms of written courtship.
Words that go before 'note'.Key: A keynote speech sets the main theme of an event. The word comes from music, where the key note defines the scale.
Words that go before 'note'.High: A high note shows off a singer's range. Mariah Carey's whistle register is famed for notes above the top of a standard piano.
Words that go before 'note'.Grace: A grace note is a quick ornamental note before the main one. Mozart and Chopin used them for decorative flourishes.
Words that go before 'note'.Side: A sidenote is an aside from the main text. A margin comment beside the page is the same idea.
Words that go before 'note'.Ransom: A ransom note demands payment for a hostage. In films it's often made of cut-out newspaper letters, a cliché.
Words that go before 'note'.Quarter: A quarter note lasts one beat in 4/4 time. In the UK it's called a crotchet, from a French word for hook.
Words that go before 'note'.Whole: A whole note, a semibreve in British English, is the longest common note. It lasts four beats in 4/4 time.
Words that go before 'note'.Book: Notebook is a word, but book note is not. The order of the words only works one way.
Words that go before 'note'.Pad: Pad note isn't a phrase, though notepad is. The words work only in the opposite order.
Words that go before 'note'.Chair: Chair note isn't a word. A chair can have a cushion or arms, but nothing to do with notes.
Words that go before 'note'.Pen: Pen note isn't a standard phrase. Penknife and pen name exist, but a pen note does not.
Words that go before 'note'.Table: Table note doesn't work, though table talk does. Notes can be put on a table, but they aren't named for one.
Words that go before 'note'.Shoe: Shoe note isn't a word. Shoes have shoelaces and shoehorns, but no notes.
Words that go before 'note'.Dog: Dog note isn't a phrase. Dogs can hear much higher notes than humans, which is how silent dog whistles work.
Words that go before 'note'.Window: Window note isn't used. Windows do appear in a sticky note stuck on one, but not as a compound.
Words that go before 'note'.Coffee: Coffee note isn't a phrase, though in tasting, a coffee can have notes of chocolate or fruit.
Words that go before 'note'.Moon: Moon note isn't a phrase. Moonlight Sonata has notes, but the compound isn't used.
Words that go before 'note'.Tree: Tree note isn't a word. A Christmas tree might have a note card hung on it, but the phrase isn't used.
Words that go before 'note'.River: River note isn't a word. A river can sound musical, but nobody calls it a note.
