Songs with a month in the title.April Come She Will: Simon and Garfunkel's gentle song walks through the months from April to September, a poem set to a quiet guitar.
Songs with a month in the title.November Rain: Guns N' Roses' 1991 epic runs almost nine minutes and its video was among the most expensive ever made.
Songs with a month in the title.October: U2's 1981 second album has this title song, which is a short piano piece.
Songs with a month in the title.Back to December: Taylor Swift wrote it in 2010, a rare apology song, thought to be about Taylor Lautner.
Songs with a month in the title.December 1963: The Four Seasons' 1975 hit, subtitled "Oh, What a Night", reached No. 1 in the US.
Songs with a month in the title.August: Taylor Swift's 2020 song from "Folklore" is about a summer fling in the title month.
Songs with a month in the title.January: Pilot's hit topped the UK chart in early 1975, and it is a singalong glam-pop song named for a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Cold December Night: Michael Bublé's 2011 seasonal single is one of his Christmas songs from the album.
Songs with a month in the title.In the Summertime: Mungo Jerry's 1970 hit has a season, not a month, in its title.
Songs with a month in the title.Autumn Leaves: This jazz standard comes from the French song "Les Feuilles mortes", and its title names a season, not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Winter Wonderland: A 1934 song with a season in the title, but not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Here Comes the Sun: George Harrison wrote it in Eric Clapton's garden, with no month in the title.
Songs with a month in the title.Easter Parade: Irving Berlin's 1933 song is named for a holiday and not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.This Is Halloween: It's from "The Nightmare Before Christmas", a holiday and not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Summer of '69: It names a season and a year, not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Manic Monday: The Bangles hit names a day of the week, not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Yesterday: The Beatles' song names no month, and Paul McCartney reportedly dreamed the tune.
Songs with a month in the title.Eight Days a Week: The Beatles' 1964 song is named after a chauffeur's remark about working eight days a week, and it names no month.
Songs with a month in the title.Hey Jude: The Beatles' 1968 single lasts over seven minutes, and it has no month in the title.
Songs with a month in the title.Purple Rain: Prince's title song is about a color, not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Ruby Tuesday: The Stones' 1967 title names a weekday, not a month.
Songs with a month in the title.Wonderwall: Oasis's 1995 hit has no month, and the name comes from a George Harrison film.
Songs with a month in the title.Tomorrow: It's a famous song from "Annie", but it names no month.

Tennis players.Serena Williams: Won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most in the Open era, and won one while pregnant, the 2017 Australian Open.
Tennis players.Roger Federer: Won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, including eight Wimbledons, and spent 237 consecutive weeks at world number one.
Tennis players.Rafael Nadal: The 'King of Clay' won the French Open a record 14 times, and finished with 22 Grand Slam titles.
Tennis players.Novak Djokovic: Holds the record of 24 Grand Slam singles titles, and spent more weeks at world number one than anyone.
Tennis players.Andy Murray: Ended Britain's 77-year wait for a men's Wimbledon champion in 2013, and won Olympic singles gold twice.
Tennis players.Venus Williams: Won seven Grand Slam singles titles, and was among the first to successfully push for equal prize money at Wimbledon in 2007.
Tennis players.Steffi Graf: The only player to win a Golden Slam, all four majors and Olympic gold in the same year, 1988.
Tennis players.Bjorn Borg: Swedish star who won five straight Wimbledons from 1976 to 1980, retiring at only 26.
Tennis players.John McEnroe: Famous for his temper and the phrase 'You cannot be serious!', and he won seven Grand Slam singles titles.
Tennis players.Coco Gauff: Reached Wimbledon's fourth round at 15 after beating Venus Williams, and won the 2023 US Open.
Tennis players.Carlos Alcaraz: A Spaniard who won the US Open at 19 in 2022 to become the youngest world number one.
Tennis players.Pete Sampras: Won 14 Grand Slam titles, including seven Wimbledons, and was known for his serve and volley.
Tennis players.Andre Agassi: Won all four Grand Slams and an Olympic gold, completing a Career Golden Slam, and wore denim shorts in the early 1990s.
Tennis players.Tiger Woods: A golfer, not tennis, with 15 major championships.
Tennis players.Michael Jordan: A basketball star, who won six NBA titles with Chicago, and tried baseball briefly.
Tennis players.Lionel Messi: A soccer star who won the 2022 World Cup with Argentina.
Tennis players.Usain Bolt: A sprinter, who holds the 100 m record of 9.58 seconds, not a tennis player.
Tennis players.Michael Phelps: A swimmer with 23 Olympic gold medals, the most ever.
Tennis players.Simone Biles: A gymnast, and the most decorated in world championships history.
Tennis players.Wayne Gretzky: An ice hockey star nicknamed 'The Great One', who holds many NHL records, including the most career points.
Tennis players.Tom Brady: A football quarterback with seven Super Bowl wins, the most of any player.
Tennis players.Babe Ruth: A baseball icon, who hit 714 home runs, and began as a pitcher.
Tennis players.Muhammad Ali: A boxer who won the heavyweight title three times and was known for 'float like a butterfly'.
Tennis players.Lewis Hamilton: A Formula One driver with seven world championships, tied with Michael Schumacher.

Parts of a bicycle.Handlebars: The 1817 Draisine had no pedals but already used handlebars to steer.
Parts of a bicycle.Pedals: The French added them to the front wheel in the 1860s, creating the first true pedal bicycle.
Parts of a bicycle.Chain: The chain drive on the 1880s Rover safety bicycle let riders sit low and made bikes far safer.
Parts of a bicycle.Saddle: Racing saddles are narrow and hard, since riders spend long hours supported by their sit bones.
Parts of a bicycle.Spokes: A bicycle wheel hangs from the spokes at the top, so wheels work in tension, not compression.
Parts of a bicycle.Derailleur: Its name comes from the French word for derail, since it moves the chain onto other gears; the Tour allowed them in 1937.
Parts of a bicycle.Crank: The arms connecting the pedals to the chainring are commonly about 170 millimeters long.
Parts of a bicycle.Brake lever: Squeezing it pulls a cable that clamps the brake pads on the rim or disc.
Parts of a bicycle.Kickstand: The little leg that props the bike up is a convenience that racing bikes leave off to save weight.
Parts of a bicycle.Sprocket: Modern bikes may have up to 12 of these gear cogs on the back wheel.
Parts of a bicycle.Frame: The top carbon road frames can weigh under a kilogram and still handle huge forces.
Parts of a bicycle.Inner tube: John Boyd Dunlop reinvented the pneumatic tire in 1888 for his son's tricycle.
Parts of a bicycle.Bell: In the UK new bikes must be sold with one, and many countries have similar rules.
Parts of a bicycle.Steering wheel: Cars steer with a wheel, bikes use handlebars, a trap as the shape looks similar.
Parts of a bicycle.Exhaust pipe: It carries engine exhaust away, which bikes don't have unless motorized.
Parts of a bicycle.Spark plug: The spark plug ignites fuel in a gasoline engine, and a bicycle has no engine.
Parts of a bicycle.Carburetor: The carburetor mixes air and fuel in older engines, but bikes run on legs.
Parts of a bicycle.Windshield: A windshield shields drivers from wind, which cyclists feel with their face.
Parts of a bicycle.Gearstick: The gearstick shifts a car's gears, while bikes use shifters on the handlebars.
Parts of a bicycle.Oar: Oars row boats, which are propelled by water, not by chains.
Parts of a bicycle.Rudder: A rudder steers a ship or a boat from the back and is not found on bikes.
Parts of a bicycle.Mast: The mast holds a sailboat's sails and is not part of a bicycle.
Parts of a bicycle.Propeller: A propeller drives boats and planes, and a bike's pedals do not drive one.
Parts of a bicycle.Clutch pedal: Bikes have pedals too, but this one is the car's gear pedal and not part of a bicycle.

Archery words.Bow: One of humanity's oldest tools; archaeological evidence suggests bows were in use over 10,000 years ago.
Archery words.Arrow: Modern target arrows are made of carbon or aluminium, and at the Olympics they fly at about 200 km/h.
Archery words.Quiver: Holds spare arrows at the hip or back, and the word also means to tremble, from a separate origin.
Archery words.Bullseye: The centre ring of a target; on an Olympic target it is only 12 cm across, shot from 70 metres.
Archery words.Fletching: The feathers or vanes on an arrow's tail, which spin the shaft for stable flight; the word comes from the French for arrow, fleche.
Archery words.Nock: The notch at the arrow's rear, which sits on the string, and also the name for the act of fitting it.
Archery words.Bowstring: Modern ones are of high-strength synthetic fibre, and a string is usually made of many strands twisted together.
Archery words.Arm guard: Worn on the forearm to protect from the string's slap, which can bruise badly if the bow arm isn't held right.
Archery words.Target: Olympic target faces are 122 cm wide, with ten scoring rings, and they use a blue, red, gold colour set.
Archery words.Longbow: The English weapon that helped win Agincourt in 1415, and archers trained from childhood to draw its heavy pull.
Archery words.Recurve: The only bow style used at the Olympics, with limbs that curve away at the tips to give more power.
Archery words.Compound bow: Pulleys, called cams, reduce the holding weight at full draw, so archers can hold and aim steadily.
Archery words.Oche: The line that darts players stand behind when throwing, and an odd word of unknown origin.
Archery words.Flights: The wings at the tail of a dart, which keep it stable, and the term is not from archery.
Archery words.Cue: A pool or snooker stick, and cue sports use balls not arrows.
Archery words.Puck: The hard rubber disc in ice hockey, which can be shot at over 100 mph.
Archery words.Wicket: The cricket stumps and bails, a target that the bowler tries to hit.
Archery words.Shuttlecock: A feathered projectile in badminton, which can travel at speeds over 400 km/h in smashes.
Archery words.Javelin: A throwing spear in track and field, and a weapon, but not the archer's arrow.
Archery words.Discus: A throwing disc in athletics, nothing to do with archery.
Archery words.Foil: A light fencing blade, which is a sword rather than a bow.
Archery words.Epee: A fencing sword that is the heaviest of the three weapons, and has no relation to archery.
Archery words.Spear: A hand-thrown or thrust weapon, and unlike an arrow it needs no bow.
Archery words.Hammer: The ball on a wire thrown in athletics, which weighs 7.26 kg for men.

Pencil-and-paper games.Tic-tac-toe: With perfect play it always ends in a draw, so the whole game fits in a tiny tree. In Britain it's noughts and crosses.
Pencil-and-paper games.Hangman: A guessing game of blanks and a growing gallows. Opening with E, the most common English letter, is the classic best first guess.
Pencil-and-paper games.Dots and boxes: Players join dots and claim boxes by closing them. French mathematician Edouard Lucas described it in 1889 as la pipopipette.
Pencil-and-paper games.MASH: Mansion, Apartment, Shack, House: a spiral drawn until you stop decides your future home, spouse and car.
Pencil-and-paper games.Consequences: A Victorian parlour game where players write parts of a story on folded paper and pass it on. Surrealists adapted it as Exquisite Corpse.
Pencil-and-paper games.Sprouts: A topology game invented in 1967 at Cambridge by John Conway and Michael Paterson. It always ends within a fixed number of moves.
Pencil-and-paper games.Crossword: The first modern one appeared in the New York World on December 21, 1913, made by Arthur Wynne, who called it a word-cross.
Pencil-and-paper games.Word search: Usually credited to Norman Gibat of Oklahoma, who published the first one in 1968. The words can run in any direction.
Pencil-and-paper games.Sudoku: The name is a Japanese abbreviation. Howard Garns invented it in 1979 as Number Place, and Japan's Nikoli publisher made it famous.
Pencil-and-paper games.Connect the dots: Drawing a line through numbered points reveals a hidden picture. The idea doubles as a metaphor for seeing the pattern behind scattered facts.
Pencil-and-paper games.Charades: Silent acting, no paper needed. It began as a Victorian parlour game, and its name comes from a French word for a riddle.
Pencil-and-paper games.Jenga: Wooden blocks stacked into a tower. The name comes from Swahili kujenga, to build, and it was created by Leslie Scott in the 1970s.
Pencil-and-paper games.Uno: A card game created in 1971 by Ohio barber Merle Robbins. It needs a printed deck rather than a pencil.
Pencil-and-paper games.Twister: Made in 1966, it was a hit after Johnny Carson played it with Eva Gabor on TV. Players' bodies, not pencils, do the work.
Pencil-and-paper games.Chess: Chess needs a physical board and pieces. The number of possible games vastly outnumbers the atoms in the observable universe.
Pencil-and-paper games.Checkers: Played with discs on a board. In 2007 a team led by Jonathan Schaeffer proved that with perfect play checkers is a draw.
Pencil-and-paper games.Tag: A running-around chase game with no pencil. The Britons call it tig, and it needs space more than paper.
Pencil-and-paper games.Marbles: Glass marbles became mass-produced after German marble scissors arrived in the 1840s. Flicked across the floor, not drawn on paper.
Pencil-and-paper games.Jacks: Played with a small ball and metal stars. Older versions used animal knucklebones, hence the alternate name knucklebones.
Pencil-and-paper games.Dominoes: Tiles marked with dots, matched end to end. They reached Europe in the 1700s and need no pencil unless you're keeping score.
Pencil-and-paper games.Hide and seek: Hiding games like this appear in ancient Greek writings. Nothing on paper, just a good hiding spot.
Pencil-and-paper games.Simon Says: Obey only commands that begin with 'Simon says'. It predates the 1978 electronic Simon toy and needs ears, not pencils.
Pencil-and-paper games.Rock paper scissors: Played with hand shapes. A World Rock Paper Scissors Society runs championships, but you only need hands.
Pencil-and-paper games.Musical chairs: Walk around the chairs until the music stops, with one fewer chair than players. It tests reflexes, not penmanship.

What a medieval knight would wear.Chainmail: Interlinked iron rings protected against slashing blows. A full shirt could weigh around 10 kg and take months to make.
What a medieval knight would wear.Helmet: Knights' helmets evolved from simple caps to full visored "great helms," and a small slit for sight left them with limited vision.
What a medieval knight would wear.Gauntlets: Armored gloves of plate and leather. Throwing one down was a formal challenge, the origin of "throwing down the gauntlet."
What a medieval knight would wear.Breastplate: Plate armor protecting the chest, shaped to deflect lance strikes. Full plate armor was less heavy than many assume, about 20 to 25 kg.
What a medieval knight would wear.Surcoat: A cloth tunic worn over armor, often showing the knight's heraldry. It helped identify friend from foe and shielded metal from the sun.
What a medieval knight would wear.Spurs: Metal prongs on the heel used to urge a horse on. Being a knight was called "winning one's spurs."
What a medieval knight would wear.Greaves: Plates guarding the shins and lower legs. Ancient Greek soldiers wore them too, so this is armor with a very long history.
What a medieval knight would wear.Gambeson: A thick quilted jacket worn under mail to absorb blows. Alone, it was often the main armor of ordinary soldiers.
What a medieval knight would wear.Sabatons: Armored shoes of overlapping steel plates protecting the feet. Their pointed toes were sometimes long in fashion.
What a medieval knight would wear.Pauldrons: Plate armor for the shoulders. Their name comes from a French word for shoulder, and they protected a joint that was easy to hit.
What a medieval knight would wear.Toga: A Roman civilian garment, about a thousand years before knights. It would be useless against a sword.
What a medieval knight would wear.Kimono: A traditional Japanese robe, not European. Samurai wore armor in battle, and knights in Europe never saw one.
What a medieval knight would wear.Sneakers: Rubber-soled athletic shoes arrived in the 19th century. A medieval knight wore leather shoes or armored sabatons.
What a medieval knight would wear.Top hat: A tall silk hat of the 1800s gentleman. Knights lived hundreds of years earlier.
What a medieval knight would wear.Tuxedo: Named after Tuxedo Park, New York, where the style became popular in the 1880s. It's far too late for the Middle Ages.
What a medieval knight would wear.Hoodie: Modern sportswear with roots in 1930s workwear. Medieval monks wore hoods, but not knights.
What a medieval knight would wear.Jeans: Denim work trousers made famous in 1870s California. They were not medieval, since denim pants came centuries later.
What a medieval knight would wear.Sombrero: A wide-brimmed Mexican hat whose name means "shade-maker." Medieval Europe never saw one.
What a medieval knight would wear.Baseball cap: A cap invented in the 1860s for baseball. It would be centuries too late for a knight.
What a medieval knight would wear.Wristwatch: Wristwatches only became common around the First World War. Knights had no personal timepieces.
What a medieval knight would wear.Flip-flops: Though sandals like them are ancient, flip-flops are a modern invention. Knights wore sturdy leather boots.
What a medieval knight would wear.Bow tie: A neckwear that rose from 17th-century Croatian soldiers' cravats, so it's a few centuries after the knights.
What a medieval knight would wear.Raincoat: Waterproof rubberized coats came with Macintosh in the 1820s. Knights relied on wool cloaks for rain.
What a medieval knight would wear.Tracksuit: Tracksuits are a 20th-century sports outfit, popularized in the 1970s. Knights' training gear was padded gambesons and wooden swords.

Monarchs of England or the UK.Henry VIII: England's king from 1509 to 1547, with six wives. He broke with Rome to form the Church of England so that he could annul his first marriage.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Elizabeth I: Reigned 1558 to 1603, a time that saw the defeat of the Spanish Armada and Shakespeare. She never married, and was called the Virgin Queen.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Victoria: Queen for 63 years, from 1837 to 1901, until Elizabeth II surpassed her. She gave her name to an era and became empress of India in 1876.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Richard III: Killed at Bosworth in 1485, the last English king to die in battle. His skeleton was found under a Leicester car park in 2012.
Monarchs of England or the UK.William I: William the Conqueror won at Hastings in 1066 and then ordered the Domesday Book survey in 1086. He spoke Norman French, not English.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Edward I: "Longshanks", who conquered Wales and built great castles there. He also campaigned against the Scots and earned the nickname Hammer of the Scots.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Mary I: Queen from 1553 to 1558, and the first to rule England in her own right. She was nicknamed Bloody Mary for burning Protestants.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Charles I: Was beheaded in 1649 after losing the Civil War, the only English king executed. He wore two shirts so he would not appear to shiver.
Monarchs of England or the UK.George III: Reigned 1760 to 1820, during the American Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars. He suffered bouts of illness, and his son served as Regent.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Henry V: The victor at Agincourt in 1415, who died of illness at 35. Shakespeare gave him the "band of brothers" speech.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Elizabeth II: The longest-reigning British monarch, from 1952 to 2022, a span of over 70 years. She became queen at 25 while in Kenya.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Edward VII: Victoria's son, king from 1901 to 1910. He waited nearly 60 years as heir, and gave his name to the Edwardian era.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Louis XIV: The Sun King of France, who ruled for 72 years and built Versailles. He is French, not British.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Napoleon: French emperor and military genius, who was exiled to the British island of St Helena. He was never king of England.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Charlemagne: King of the Franks and emperor of the West from AD 800, whose realm covered much of Western Europe. He was not English.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Peter the Great: Russian tsar who built St Petersburg and modernised Russia. He once worked in English shipyards, but was never an English monarch.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Catherine the Great: Russian empress, in power from 1762 to 1796. German-born, she led Russia's expansion, and was no British queen.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Robert the Bruce: King of Scots who won at Bannockburn in 1314. He was Scottish, so he was not an English monarch, though the crowns united later.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Mary Queen of Scots: Scotland's queen, who was executed by Elizabeth I in 1587. She was Scottish, and her son James later became king of England.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Frederick the Great: King of Prussia, from 1740 to 1786, a patron of Enlightenment, and a flautist. He was Prussian, not British.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Isabella I: Queen of Castile, who sponsored Columbus in 1492. She was Spanish, not English, though her daughter Catherine married Henry VIII.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Wilhelm II: The last German kaiser, who was Queen Victoria's grandson. He abdicated in 1918, but never ruled Britain.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Macbeth: A real Scottish king who ruled 1040 to 1057. Shakespeare's play distorts him, and he was never an English monarch.
Monarchs of England or the UK.Ivan the Terrible: Russia's first tsar, who ruled from 1547. He was proposed as husband to Elizabeth I, but was never English.

Naval battles.Trafalgar: In 1805 Nelson destroyed the French and Spanish fleets off Spain, though he died in the fight.
Naval battles.Salamis: In 480 BC the Greeks beat a larger Persian fleet in narrow waters near Athens.
Naval battles.Actium: The 31 BC sea fight between Octavian and Antony ended the Roman Republic's last civil war.
Naval battles.Lepanto: In 1571 a Holy League fleet beat the Ottomans in the last big galley battle, where Cervantes was wounded.
Naval battles.Midway: In 1942 US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers in one of history's decisive naval battles.
Naval battles.Jutland: The 1916 clash of British and German fleets was the largest battleship battle ever, and both sides claimed victory.
Naval battles.Navarino: In 1827 a British, French and Russian fleet destroyed an Ottoman one, among the last big battles under sail.
Naval battles.Coral Sea: In 1942 it was the first carrier battle in which the opposing ships never sighted each other.
Naval battles.Leyte Gulf: The 1944 battle is often called the largest naval battle in history, and saw the first organized kamikaze attacks.
Naval battles.Battle of the Nile: In 1798 Nelson wiped out the French fleet at Aboukir Bay, stranding Napoleon's army in Egypt.
Naval battles.Tsushima: In 1905 Japan destroyed Russia's fleet, shocking the world as an Asian power beat a European one.
Naval battles.Hampton Roads: In 1862 the ironclads Monitor and Virginia fought to a draw, and wooden warships became obsolete.
Naval battles.Waterloo: Napoleon's 1815 defeat was on land in Belgium, not at sea, and over 300 miles from the nearest big fleet.
Naval battles.Hastings: A land battle fought in 1066 on a hill in southern England, with no fleet involved.
Naval battles.Gettysburg: A land battle of the American Civil War in Pennsylvania, hundreds of miles from the ocean.
Naval battles.Agincourt: An English victory won on a muddy French field in 1415, with no ships involved.
Naval battles.Thermopylae: A land fight in a narrow pass in 480 BC, though the Greek fleet fought nearby at Artemisium.
Naval battles.Stalingrad: A huge land battle of 1942 to 1943 in a Russian city on the Volga, far from any ocean.
Naval battles.Somme: A land battle of 1916 in northern France, fought in trenches, not at sea.
Naval battles.Marathon: A land battle in 490 BC on an Athenian plain. Its name now belongs to the footrace.
Naval battles.Bunker Hill: A 1775 Revolutionary War hill fight near Boston, on land, with the key fighting on Breed's Hill.
Naval battles.Culloden: A 1746 land battle on a Scottish moor, where the Jacobite rising ended, with no ships involved.
Naval battles.Austerlitz: Napoleon's 1805 land victory in today's Czech Republic, fought the same year as Trafalgar's sea battle.
Naval battles.Cannae: Hannibal's 216 BC victory over Rome was a land battle, a masterpiece of surrounding an enemy army.

Things you might carry in a handbag.Lipstick: The modern push-up lipstick tube dates to the early 20th century; earlier lip color came in pots or paper-wrapped sticks.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Wallet: Wallets existed long before paper money, as pouches for coins; folding billfolds took off once banknotes spread.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Keys: The pin-tumbler design in most key locks traces to ancient Egypt, and Linus Yale Jr. refined it in the 1860s.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Sunglasses: Inuit made snow goggles from bone and wood with narrow slits to cut glare thousands of years ago.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Phone: Today's phone has far more computing power than the Apollo guidance computer.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Tissues: Kleenex began in 1924 as a disposable cold-cream remover; customers started using it as a handkerchief.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Hand cream: Palms have no oil glands, which is why hands dry out so easily and hand cream is popular.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Hairbrush: Boar-bristle brushes are prized for spreading the scalp's natural oils along the length of hair.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Mints: Peppermint is a natural hybrid of watermint and spearmint.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Compact mirror: Early mirrors were polished stone or metal; glass backed with silver became standard in the 1800s.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Folding umbrella: Umbrellas were used for shade in ancient Egypt, China and Assyria long before anyone used one for rain.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Pen: A single ballpoint can write a line roughly two kilometers long before the ink runs out.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Lip balm: Commercial lip balm sticks date to the late 1800s, long before today's brands.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Toaster: Charles Strite patented the pop-up toaster in 1919, but it would never fit in a purse.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Lawnmower: The tidy lawn became a status symbol in 17th-century France and England; no one carries a mower in a purse.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Ironing board: Sarah Boone patented an improved ironing board in 1892, designed to shape garment sleeves.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Bathtub: Archimedes' 'Eureka' tale has him noticing displaced water while stepping into a bath; the tub itself stays home.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Bookshelf: IKEA's Billy bookcase has sold in the tens of millions, but not one has fit in a handbag.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Microwave: The first Radarange of 1947 was about 1.8 meters tall and weighed hundreds of kilograms.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Ladder: In Jacob's dream a ladder reached heaven, but it's way too long for a purse.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Fridge: Early refrigerators leaked toxic gases until Freon arrived in the 1930s, and they're certainly not handbag-sized.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Sofa: 'Sofa' comes from the Arabic suffa, a raised platform for sitting.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Vacuum cleaner: Hubert Cecil Booth built a huge horse-drawn petrol vacuum in 1901 that cleaned buildings from the street.
Things you might carry in a handbag.Bicycle: Absurdly large, though folding bicycles exist that fold into a package roughly the size of a big bag.

Things you do with your mouth.Chew: Chewing starts digestion before you swallow, since saliva already begins breaking down starch in the mouth.
Things you do with your mouth.Whistle: Whistling works by forcing air through a small opening in your lips, so mouth shape alone sets the pitch.
Things you do with your mouth.Lick: Licking brings flavor molecules into contact with thousands of taste buds spread across your tongue.
Things you do with your mouth.Yawn: Yawning is contagious, even from reading about it, and scientists still debate exactly why we do it.
Things you do with your mouth.Sing: Singing shapes vowels with your mouth, and choir singers' heartbeats can even drift into sync during a song.
Things you do with your mouth.Smile: A genuine smile uses muscles around the eyes as well as the mouth, known as a Duchenne smile.
Things you do with your mouth.Bite: Human bites are mild compared with a crocodile's, which is among the strongest bite forces ever measured.
Things you do with your mouth.Sip: Tea and wine tasters sip with a loud slurp on purpose, spreading the liquid and aroma through the mouth.
Things you do with your mouth.Gargle: The word gargle comes from the French for throat, and the bubbling is air passing through liquid held at the back of your mouth.
Things you do with your mouth.Spit: Your mouth makes about a liter of saliva a day, so there's always plenty ready to spit.
Things you do with your mouth.Pout: Pouting pushes out the lower lip, and Darwin noted that sulking children in many cultures do it.
Things you do with your mouth.Slurp: In Japan, slurping noodles is a polite way to show enjoyment, and it also cools them and enhances the flavor.
Things you do with your mouth.Swallow: Swallowing takes dozens of muscles working in sequence, and you can do it upside down because muscles push, not gravity.
Things you do with your mouth.Wink: Winking uses the eyelid muscles, though many people find they can't stop their mouths twitching along with it.
Things you do with your mouth.Blink: The average person blinks around 15 to 20 times a minute, but it's your eyelids, not your mouth, that do it.
Things you do with your mouth.Clap: Clapping is a hand action, and the sound comes from air squeezed out between the palms.
Things you do with your mouth.Shrug: Shrugging is mostly shoulders, and it's a gesture people use everywhere to say they don't know.
Things you do with your mouth.Nod: Nodding is done with the neck and head, and its meaning famously flips in places like Bulgaria.
Things you do with your mouth.Tiptoe: Tiptoeing keeps your weight on the balls of your feet, which is why it's quieter and a favorite of cartoon burglars.
Things you do with your mouth.Sniff: Sniffing is a nose job: it pulls air up toward smell receptors high in the nasal cavity that ordinary breathing barely reaches.
Things you do with your mouth.Squint: Squinting is an eye move: narrowing the lids cuts stray light and briefly sharpens your focus.
Things you do with your mouth.Snap: A finger snap is done with the hand, and despite looking leisurely it happens in only a few milliseconds.
Things you do with your mouth.Kick: Kicking is a leg job, and in soccer a hard kick can send the ball flying over 100 kilometers per hour.
Things you do with your mouth.Wave: Waving uses the hand and arm, and the royal family's famous slow wave is a deliberately small, tidy one.

Things you can fold.Paper: Origami, the Japanese art of paper folding, creates figures without cutting; but a sheet of paper can't be folded in half more than about 7 times.
Things you can fold.Towel: Towels fold flat for storage, and hotels often twist them into animal shapes called towel origami for guests.
Things you can fold.T-shirt: Folding a T-shirt flat in seconds is possible with the famous two-pinch Japanese method, which people like to use for tidy drawers.
Things you can fold.Napkin: Napkin folding is an old dining art; in the 1600s and 1700s elaborate designs, from swans to ships, decorated European banquet tables.
Things you can fold.Road map: Folding a paper road map correctly back into its original creases defeated generations of drivers, and the mathematician Miura devised a fold that opens in one pull.
Things you can fold.Blanket: Blankets fold into neat squares for storage, and the name comes from the French blanchet, a white woolen cloth.
Things you can fold.Bedsheet: Hospital corners are the folding style nurses use for tight, neat bed sheets that stay put.
Things you can fold.Letter: Letters used to be folded into their own envelope with wax seals, before gummed envelopes became common in the 1800s.
Things you can fold.Folding chair: The folding chair has existed since ancient Egypt and Rome, where the folding stool, called a sella curulis, signaled high rank.
Things you can fold.Pocketknife: A pocketknife has a blade that folds into the handle; the famous Swiss Army knife began in 1891 with a soldier's model.
Things you can fold.Jeans: Jeans are typically folded along the seams and kept in stacks, and denim gets its name from the French serge de Nimes.
Things you can fold.Tortilla: Tortillas fold around fillings into tacos and burritos, and they are one of Mexico's oldest foods, made from corn for thousands of years.
Things you can fold.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is a solid slab of resin or plastic, and any bend would crack it, so there is nothing foldable about it.
Things you can fold.Brick: Fired clay is hard and brittle, so a brick snaps under a bend rather than folding; masons cut bricks by tapping to crack them.
Things you can fold.Glass bottle: At room temperature, glass breaks instead of bending, which is why bottles are shaped by heating the glass until it is soft.
Things you can fold.Piano: A concert grand weighs around 500 kilograms and its iron frame carries tons of string tension, so folding one is impossible.
Things you can fold.Boulder: Solid rock cracks rather than folds, though over millions of years entire layers of rock can fold when pushed by tectonic forces.
Things you can fold.Coconut: A coconut's hard shell and tough fibers resist folding, and the husk is so strong it is used to make rope and mats.
Things you can fold.Light bulb: A light bulb is delicate thin glass sealed around a filament, so the slightest bend would shatter it.
Things you can fold.Marble: Marble is a hard stone that splits when bent, although deep underground, intense heat and pressure can fold even marble over geologic time.
Things you can fold.Teapot: A rigid teapot of ceramic or cast iron can't fold, although some camping kettles use silicone that collapses flat.
Things you can fold.Doorknob: A doorknob is solid metal or glass that holds its shape, and if you force it to bend, it will break off.
Things you can fold.Anvil: An anvil is a block of hardened steel built to absorb hammer blows without bending, so it is the opposite of foldable.
Things you can fold.Billiard ball: Billiard balls were once carved from ivory and are now made of hard phenolic resin, so they crack before they would ever bend.

Things that would wake you up.Alarm clock: The first mechanical alarm clock is credited to Levi Hutchins in 1787, but it only rang at 4 a.m., his daily wake time.
Things that would wake you up.Rooster: A rooster crows because of an internal body clock, and it can crow before dawn, not just at sunrise.
Things that would wake you up.Thunder: Thunder is the sound of air heated to about five times the sun's surface temperature by lightning.
Things that would wake you up.Smoke alarm: A smoke alarm's piercing beep is tuned to about 3,000 hertz, a pitch that wakes sleepers best.
Things that would wake you up.Barking dog: Dogs bark for many reasons, and a dog's bark can wake a house even when other sounds do not.
Things that would wake you up.Car alarm: Car alarms are famously ignored, as most false alarms have taught neighbors to tune them out.
Things that would wake you up.Doorbell: The first electric doorbell was patented in 1831 by the American scientist Joseph Henry, and it still wakes sleepers today.
Things that would wake you up.Bucket of water: A bucket of cold water is the classic rude awakening, and cold shocks trigger a gasp reflex.
Things that would wake you up.Jackhammer: A jackhammer can reach over 100 decibels, loud enough to damage hearing in minutes, and it will wake anyone.
Things that would wake you up.Crying baby: A baby's cry is tuned to be hard to ignore, and it is even more effective at waking parents than other noises.
Things that would wake you up.Garbage truck: A garbage truck's hydraulics and clanging can top 80 decibels, loud enough to wake neighbors every collection day.
Things that would wake you up.Siren: A siren's wailing pitch rises and falls, and its sweep makes it harder for the brain to tune out.
Things that would wake you up.Lullaby: Lullabies have been sung to children for thousands of years, and a slow rhythm tends to slow breathing.
Things that would wake you up.White noise: White noise masks sudden sounds with a steady hiss, and it can help people fall asleep faster.
Things that would wake you up.Pillow: Pillows have existed since ancient Mesopotamia, and early ones were stone, so a soft one is a modern luxury.
Things that would wake you up.Blanket: A blanket traps your body heat, and a heavier one is said to calm many people through gentle pressure.
Things that would wake you up.Teddy bear: The teddy bear is named for Theodore Roosevelt, after a 1902 hunting trip where he refused to shoot a captive bear.
Things that would wake you up.Eye mask: An eye mask blocks light, and light is the strongest signal telling your brain it's time to wake.
Things that would wake you up.Earplugs: Foam earplugs can reduce noise by about 30 decibels, and the ancient Greeks reportedly used wax.
Things that would wake you up.Chamomile tea: Chamomile tea is a long-time bedtime drink, and a compound called apigenin may mildly promote drowsiness.
Things that would wake you up.Warm milk: Warm milk contains tryptophan, but the amount is small, so its sleepy effect is mostly ritual and comfort.
Things that would wake you up.Night light: A dim night light is gentle enough not to shut off melatonin, unlike bright blue light, so it will not wake you.
Things that would wake you up.Counting sheep: Counting sheep is an old bedtime trick, and studies found that picturing a calm scene may work better.
Things that would wake you up.Soft music: Slow soft music at about 60 beats per minute can help the body relax, as it matches a resting heart rate.

Workers who work mainly with wood.Carpenter: Carpenters build wooden structures, from roof frames to floors, and many wooden joints work without a single nail.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Joiner: Joiners make fitted wooden items like doors and stairs, often using joints that hold without screws.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Cabinetmaker: Cabinetmakers build fine furniture, and the term was first used in the 1600s for makers of cabinets, meaning small private rooms.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks fell trees, and in the old days they drove logs down rivers, balancing on the floating timber.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Cooper: Coopers make barrels from curved staves held by hoops, with no glue, and the craft remains central to whisky and wine.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Wheelwright: Wheelwrights made wooden cartwheels, and their name remains a surname, like Wright, which is just worker in wood.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Woodturner: Woodturners shape wood on a lathe, and a good bowl can be turned from a single piece in minutes.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Luthier: Luthiers make stringed instruments such as violins and guitars, and the word comes from lute, an old plucked instrument.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Sawyer: Sawyers cut logs into planks, often in a pit with one man below and one on top, a hard job and one of the oldest in the trade.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Woodcarver: Woodcarvers shape wood with chisels, and some medieval church carvings have lasted over 700 years.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Glazier: Glaziers fit glass into windows, though they often work with wooden frames rather than shaping wood.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Blacksmith: Blacksmiths shape hot iron by hammering, and the word comes from black, the colour of iron, which smiths work.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Potter: Potters shape clay on a wheel or by hand, and pottery shards are among the oldest human-made objects.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Tanner: Tanners turn animal hides into leather, a smelly business that was often placed outside medieval towns.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Stonemason: Stonemasons carve stone, so they don't work with wood at all, and have worked on pyramids and cathedrals.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Tailor: Tailors cut and sew cloth into clothing, so their raw material is fabric, not wood.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Cobbler: Cobblers repair shoes, and use leather and glue, not timber, though old shoe lasts were made of wood.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Plumber: Plumbers work with pipes, and wooden pipes were used in past times, but modern plumbers use plastic and copper.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Welder: Welders join metal by heat, so they work with steel and not with wood.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Jeweler: Jewelers craft ornaments from gold, silver and stones, and their work is at a very small scale.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Weaver: Weavers make cloth on a loom, and the loom is one of the oldest human tools.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Chandler: Chandlers made candles, and later the word came to mean a ship supplies dealer, rather than a woodworker.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Milliner: Milliners make hats, and the word comes from Milan, famed for fashion goods in the 1500s.
Workers who work mainly with wood.Upholsterer: Upholsterers pad and cover seating, and while they work with wooden frames, their main material is fabric and stuffing.

Things a lifeguard uses.Whistle: Whistle codes vary by place, but a long blast usually clears the water and several short ones raise an alarm.
Things a lifeguard uses.Rescue tube: A foam torpedo on a strap keeps both lifeguard and swimmer afloat during a rescue.
Things a lifeguard uses.Buoy: Bright buoys mark safe swimming zones, and a ring buoy thrown from shore is among the quickest rescues.
Things a lifeguard uses.Lookout tower: The height widens the view, and lifeguard training stresses scanning each zone every 10 seconds.
Things a lifeguard uses.Binoculars: Guards scan for signs of a struggling swimmer, since real drowning is usually quiet and rarely looks like waving and shouting.
Things a lifeguard uses.First aid kit: Beyond bandages, beach kits are stocked for common problems like jellyfish stings, cuts and heat illness.
Things a lifeguard uses.Sunscreen: Lifeguards spend whole shifts outdoors, and the white zinc-oxide nose is a classic lifeguard look.
Things a lifeguard uses.Megaphone: Samuel Morland made the speaking trumpet in the 1670s, an ancestor of the megaphone.
Things a lifeguard uses.Rescue board: A paddleboard-style board lets guards cross surf quickly, and lifesaving clubs in Australia race on them.
Things a lifeguard uses.Two-way radio: Radios link towers along a beach, so one guard's rescue is backed up by others still watching the water.
Things a lifeguard uses.Fishing rod: A reaching pole is a lifeguard's rod, but a fishing rod would hook the swimmer.
Things a lifeguard uses.Spear gun: A tool for underwater hunting, and a hazard on crowded beaches, where it is often banned.
Things a lifeguard uses.Harpoon: A barbed spear tied to a line for whales and large fish, so it is the opposite of rescue gear.
Things a lifeguard uses.Lasso: Ranchers use it for cattle, while lifeguards throw a rope bag or ring buoy.
Things a lifeguard uses.Briefcase: A lifeguard's bag carries gloves and a pocket mask, while a briefcase carries only papers.
Things a lifeguard uses.Hard hat: Construction sites require them, while lifeguards wear wide-brimmed hats and sunglasses.
Things a lifeguard uses.Gavel: A judge's tool, the kind of thing you hear in a courtroom, not on a beach.
Things a lifeguard uses.Kiln: A potter's oven that fires clay at over 1,000 degrees Celsius, the opposite of a pool.
Things a lifeguard uses.Trowel: Gardeners and bricklayers use it, though sandcastle builders might as well.
Things a lifeguard uses.Anvil: A blacksmith's block weighing from 50 to over 300 pounds, which would sink to the bottom of the pool.
Things a lifeguard uses.Pitchfork: A farmhand's hay tool, usually with three tines, nothing to do with saving swimmers.
Things a lifeguard uses.Stapler: A red Swingline stapler became a pop-culture icon in the 1999 film Office Space.
Things a lifeguard uses.Typewriter: Early typewriters in the 1870s were made by the Remington company, which also made guns.
Things a lifeguard uses.Rolling pin: A baker's tool; French pins are tapered and handle-free.

Navigation tools used before GPS.Sextant: It measures the angle between a star or the sun and the horizon to find latitude, and dates from around 1730.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Compass: Chinese compasses used lodestone for divination long before sailors adopted them around the 12th century.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Astrolabe: Medieval astronomers and sailors used it to measure the altitude of stars, and it could also tell time.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Chronometer: John Harrison's marine clocks solved the longitude problem in the 1700s by keeping accurate time at sea.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Star chart: Celestial navigation relies on charts of stars, and Polynesian navigators carried theirs in memory.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Nautical chart: Charts show depths and hazards, and the earliest ones, portolan charts, appeared in the 13th-century Mediterranean.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Dividers: A two-legged tool for measuring distance on charts by stepping the points across.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Lead line: A weighted rope sounds depth, and its tallowed base brings up samples from the seabed; Mark Twain's name comes from calling the depth.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Quadrant: An earlier ancestor of the sextant, this quarter-circle measured the height of stars.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Hourglass: Sailors used sand glasses to time a log line and so measure ship speed in knots.
Navigation tools used before GPS.GPS: The satellite network that replaced these tools orbits about 20,000 kilometers up, and the US military launched it in the 1970s.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Smartphone: It finds its position using GPS, Wi-Fi and cell towers, so it did not exist in the pre-GPS era.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Satellite phone: It calls via satellites, handy in remote places, but it was not a navigation tool before GPS.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Google Maps: Launched in 2005, long after sextants and star charts.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Sat nav: Short for satellite navigation, and a staple in British cars since the 1990s.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Drone: Many drones use GPS to hold their position, so they are post-GPS.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Tablet: Apple's iPad of 2010 popularized tablets, long after the age of the sextant.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Laptop: The Osborne 1 of 1981 was an early portable, weighing about 11 kilograms.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Smartwatch: It uses GPS satellites to track routes, so it belongs to the post-GPS world.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Bluetooth: Named after the Danish king Harald Bluetooth, who united tribes, as the technology unites devices.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Wi-Fi router: Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, contributed patents that helped make Wi-Fi possible.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Fitness tracker: It uses motion sensors and often GPS to follow your route.
Navigation tools used before GPS.QR code: Denso Wave invented it in 1994 in Japan to track car parts.
Navigation tools used before GPS.Search engine: Early ones like Archie appeared around 1990, centuries after the astrolabe.

Things a pharmacist handles.Prescriptions: Doctors' handwriting is famously poor, so pharmacists are trained to decode prescriptions and double-check doses before dispensing.
Things a pharmacist handles.Pills: Many pills are coated to hide a bitter taste or so they dissolve only in the intestine rather than the stomach.
Things a pharmacist handles.Capsules: Many capsule shells are made of gelatin, and vegetarian versions use plant cellulose instead.
Things a pharmacist handles.Pill counter: The little tray with a spatula and a pouring lip lets pharmacists count tablets into a bottle without touching them.
Things a pharmacist handles.Medicine labels: Labels list the drug, dose and warnings, and the pharmacist checks them against the prescription before handing anything over.
Things a pharmacist handles.Cough syrup: Much of a cough syrup's soothing effect comes from its thick, sugary base, which coats the throat.
Things a pharmacist handles.Inhalers: Inhalers deliver medicine straight to the lungs, so a much smaller dose works. Pharmacists often teach people to use them properly.
Things a pharmacist handles.Ointment: Ointments are greasy and stay on skin longer than water-based creams, which is why they're used on dry or cracked skin.
Things a pharmacist handles.Vaccines: In many countries pharmacists give vaccines such as flu shots, so you can get one without visiting a doctor.
Things a pharmacist handles.Eye drops: Eye drops must be sterile, and many bottles are discarded about a month after opening because bacteria can grow in them.
Things a pharmacist handles.Antibiotics: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses, so they can't treat a cold. Pharmacists stress finishing the course as prescribed.
Things a pharmacist handles.Gavel: A gavel is the small mallet of a judge or auctioneer, used to demand order. A pharmacist has no use for banging one.
Things a pharmacist handles.Easel: An easel props up a painter's canvas. Pharmacists don't paint, though they do make up colorful syrups.
Things a pharmacist handles.Saddle: Saddles go on horses and belong to the saddler's trade. They aren't something a pharmacist handles.
Things a pharmacist handles.Anvil: Pharmacists do grind things with a mortar and pestle, but pounding metal on an anvil belongs to a blacksmith.
Things a pharmacist handles.Trowel: A trowel is a small hand shovel for gardeners and bricklayers. Pharmacists use spatulas for mixing creams.
Things a pharmacist handles.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a long-handled farm tool for tossing hay. A pharmacy's tools are tiny and clean by comparison.
Things a pharmacist handles.Lasso: The lasso is a cowboy's rope with a slip-knot loop, and its name comes from the Spanish 'lazo'.
Things a pharmacist handles.Fishing rod: A fishing rod belongs on a lake. The only fishing at a pharmacy is for the right bottle on the shelf.
Things a pharmacist handles.Paint roller: A paint roller covers walls fast, which is useful for decorators. A pharmacist spreads ointment with a small spatula instead.
Things a pharmacist handles.Hacksaw: A hacksaw cuts metal and is a workshop tool. Pharmacies prefer precise scales and spatulas.
Things a pharmacist handles.Loom: A loom weaves threads into cloth, a weaver's craft. Nothing at the dispensing counter has anything to do with weaving.
Things a pharmacist handles.Kiln: A kiln fires clay at over 1,000 degrees Celsius. A pharmacy's heat sources are tiny by comparison.
Things a pharmacist handles.Staple gun: A staple gun is a handyman's tool. Pharmacists seal prescription bags with a single small stapler instead.

Units of digital storage.Byte: A byte is eight bits, enough for one letter of text. The term was coined in the 1950s by IBM engineer Werner Buchholz.
Units of digital storage.Kilobyte: A kilobyte is about a thousand bytes. The Apollo guidance computer had roughly 4 KB of erasable memory, less than this short note needs.
Units of digital storage.Megabyte: One megabyte holds roughly a minute of MP3 music, or a short novel's text. Early PCs of the 1980s often had well under a megabyte of memory.
Units of digital storage.Gigabyte: A gigabyte is about a billion bytes. In 1980, IBM's first drive to break the gigabyte barrier weighed over 500 pounds.
Units of digital storage.Terabyte: A terabyte is about a trillion bytes, enough for hundreds of hours of video. Consumer drives of this size became common in the 2010s.
Units of digital storage.Petabyte: A petabyte is a thousand terabytes. Large tech companies process data on this scale daily, and it would fill many millions of floppy disks.
Units of digital storage.Bit: A bit is a single 0 or 1, the smallest unit of data. The word is short for binary digit and was popularized by Claude Shannon in 1948.
Units of digital storage.Nibble: A nibble is four bits, half a byte. The wordplay was intentional: a small bite of a byte, also spelled "nybble."
Units of digital storage.Exabyte: An exabyte is a thousand petabytes, or a billion gigabytes. Global internet traffic now runs to many exabytes every single day.
Units of digital storage.Zettabyte: A zettabyte is a thousand exabytes, or a trillion gigabytes. Worldwide data creation passed this scale per year in the 2010s.
Units of digital storage.Hertz: Hertz measures cycles per second, named for physicist Heinrich Hertz. It describes frequency, such as a processor's speed, not how much storage you have.
Units of digital storage.Watt: A watt measures power, named after James Watt. It tells you how much energy a device uses, not how much data it holds.
Units of digital storage.Pixel: A pixel is one dot in an image, and the word comes from "picture element." It measures an image's size, not storage.
Units of digital storage.Volt: A volt measures electrical potential, named for Alessandro Volta, inventor of the battery. It's about electricity, not data.
Units of digital storage.Baud: Baud counts signal changes per second on a line, named for telegraph engineer Émile Baudot. It measures transmission rate, not stored data.
Units of digital storage.Decibel: The decibel measures sound level on a logarithmic scale, so 20 dB is not twice as loud as 10 dB. It has nothing to do with data.
Units of digital storage.Lumen: A lumen measures the light a source gives off. A common household bulb produces several hundred of them, and none of that is data.
Units of digital storage.Ohm: The ohm measures electrical resistance, named for Georg Ohm. It deals with current in circuits, not with storage.
Units of digital storage.Joule: The joule is a unit of energy: lifting an apple a meter takes about one joule. It's about energy, not data.
Units of digital storage.Ampere: The ampere measures electric current and honors André-Marie Ampère. It's about electricity, not data capacity.
Units of digital storage.Megapixel: A megapixel is a million pixels, a way to describe camera resolution. It's tempting, but it describes picture detail rather than storage.
Units of digital storage.Gigahertz: A gigahertz is a billion cycles per second, used for processor clock speeds. A tempting near-miss for gigabyte, but it measures speed, not size.
Units of digital storage.Kelvin: Kelvin is the scientific temperature scale, where zero is absolute zero. It measures heat, so it can't measure data.
Units of digital storage.Newton: The newton measures force, with about one newton being the weight of a small apple. It's a physics unit with no data connection.

Touchscreen gestures.Swipe: Swiping to unlock was a feature of the original 2007 iPhone, and later it came to define dating and social apps.
Touchscreen gestures.Pinch: Pinch to zoom was a showpiece of the original iPhone, and the multi-touch technology was based on earlier research from a company called FingerWorks.
Touchscreen gestures.Tap: The most basic gesture replaces the mouse click, and capacitive screens detect it by sensing the electrical charge of your finger.
Touchscreen gestures.Double-tap: On phones it commonly zooms into a map or photo, and on social apps it likes a post.
Touchscreen gestures.Long press: Holding a finger down on an item often brings up a hidden menu, and it works like a right-click on a computer.
Touchscreen gestures.Drag: Pressing and moving a finger lets you slide items or scroll lists, and it mimics grabbing a physical object.
Touchscreen gestures.Flick: A fast flick makes lists keep scrolling with simulated momentum, a touch that makes screens feel physical.
Touchscreen gestures.Spread: The opposite of a pinch, moving two fingers apart zooms in, which is why it is also called pinch out.
Touchscreen gestures.Rotate: Twisting two fingers lets you turn a photo or map, and the gesture needs multi-touch screens.
Touchscreen gestures.Right-click: This requires a mouse button, and its touchscreen stand-in is a long press.
Touchscreen gestures.Hover: A mouse pointer resting over something triggers tooltips, but a finger cannot hover on most phones.
Touchscreen gestures.Middle-click: Pressing the scroll wheel, often to open links in a new tab, belongs to mouse use.
Touchscreen gestures.Keystroke: A press of a key on a keyboard, and the word originated with typewriters.
Touchscreen gestures.Hotkey: A keyboard shortcut like Ctrl+C was designed to avoid reaching for the mouse.
Touchscreen gestures.Scroll wheel: Microsoft's 1996 IntelliMouse popularized it, and it is on mice rather than screens.
Touchscreen gestures.Ctrl+Alt+Delete: IBM engineer David Bradley invented it, and Bill Gates once said that making it need three keys was a mistake.
Touchscreen gestures.Alt+Tab: This keyboard shortcut cycles through open windows, so it is a keyboard combination, not something you do on a screen.
Touchscreen gestures.Mouse click: Douglas Engelbart's 1960s mouse was made of wood, and clicking comes from a physical button.
Touchscreen gestures.Num Lock: This toggle switches the number pad between digits and arrows, and it is a keyboard key.
Touchscreen gestures.Caps Lock: It descends from the typewriter's shift lock, and it is a keyboard key.
Touchscreen gestures.Double-click: This mouse action opens files and apps on desktop computers, and its speed is something you can adjust in settings.
Touchscreen gestures.Joystick: A stick with a button controls games and aircraft, and the word may have been coined by an early pilot.
Touchscreen gestures.Trackball: An upside-down mouse with a rolling ball on top, it was first used in a 1946 naval system.
Touchscreen gestures.Enter key: A keyboard key that grew from the typewriter's carriage return.

Python libraries.NumPy: The array library behind almost all scientific Python, it gives fast number crunching by doing the work in C code.
Python libraries.Pandas: The name comes from 'panel data', an economics term, and the library was created in 2008 by Wes McKinney.
Python libraries.Matplotlib: John Hunter began it in 2003 to give Python plotting like MATLAB, and he had a day job in neurobiology research.
Python libraries.Django: Named after the jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt, it grew out of a newspaper in Lawrence, Kansas.
Python libraries.Requests: Its tagline is 'HTTP for Humans', and Kenneth Reitz built it to make web requests far more readable.
Python libraries.Flask: Armin Ronacher released it in 2010, starting as an April Fools' joke that proved to be genuinely useful.
Python libraries.TensorFlow: Google Brain built it and open-sourced it in 2015, and it popularized deep learning among developers.
Python libraries.PyTorch: Meta's machine-learning library began at Facebook AI Research and is widely used in research.
Python libraries.Scikit-learn: It began as a Google Summer of Code project in 2007 and is a standard for classic machine learning.
Python libraries.Beautiful Soup: The name comes from the Alice in Wonderland song and refers to messy 'tag soup' HTML that it can still parse.
Python libraries.Pygame: Built on the SDL library, it makes writing simple 2D games in Python approachable.
Python libraries.SciPy: Pairs with NumPy for scientific tasks like optimization, signal processing and statistics.
Python libraries.React: Meta's JavaScript library for building user interfaces, not Python.
Python libraries.jQuery: John Resig released this JavaScript library in 2006, and it simplified browser scripting.
Python libraries.Lodash: A JavaScript utility library whose name is a play on underscore.
Python libraries.Express: Express is a web framework for Node.js, in JavaScript, not Python.
Python libraries.Angular: Google's JavaScript framework for web apps, not Python.
Python libraries.Vue: Evan You, a former Google engineer, created this JavaScript framework.
Python libraries.D3.js: A JavaScript library for drawing data visualizations in the browser, created by Mike Bostock.
Python libraries.Three.js: A JavaScript library that renders 3D graphics in browsers through WebGL.
Python libraries.Node.js: Ryan Dahl built this JavaScript runtime in 2009, so it is not a Python library.
Python libraries.npm: The Node package manager, used for JavaScript packages, whereas Python uses pip.
Python libraries.Webpack: A JavaScript module bundler that packs code and assets for the browser.
Python libraries.Babel: A JavaScript compiler that lets developers use new language features in older browsers.

Art movements.Cubism: Pioneered by Picasso and Braque around 1907-1912, it shows objects from several viewpoints at once, broken into geometric shapes.
Art movements.Surrealism: Founded in Paris in 1924, it aimed to unlock dreams and the unconscious; Dalí and Magritte painted its best-known images.
Art movements.Impressionism: The name comes from Monet's Impression, Sunrise; a critic used the word as an insult in 1874, and the artists adopted it.
Art movements.Baroque: Dramatic light, motion and grandeur defined this 1600s style, from Caravaggio's paintings to Bach's music.
Art movements.Dada: Born in Zurich in 1916 as a protest against World War I, it mocked logic and art itself; Duchamp's urinal is its icon.
Art movements.Fauvism: Critics dubbed Matisse and Derain's group 'les fauves' (the wild beasts) in 1905 for their shockingly bold, unnatural colors.
Art movements.Pop Art: Born in 1950s Britain and boomed in the US, it borrowed from ads and comics; Warhol and Lichtenstein are its stars.
Art movements.Futurism: Launched by Marinetti's 1909 manifesto in Italy, it celebrated speed, machines and war, and even called for burning museums.
Art movements.Expressionism: Instead of realism, it twisted shapes and colors to show feelings; Munch's The Scream is a landmark.
Art movements.Rococo: Frilly, playful and pastel, this 1700s French style gave us ornate interiors and Versailles-era frills, from the French rocaille.
Art movements.Art Nouveau: Around 1900, it spread swirling, plant-like curves across Paris Metro entrances, posters and Mucha's illustrations.
Art movements.Art Deco: Named after the 1925 Paris exhibition of decorative arts, it brought glamour, geometry and zigzags to the Chrysler Building.
Art movements.Romanticism: A reaction to the Enlightenment, it prized emotion and wild nature; Turner's storms and Delacroix are famous examples.
Art movements.Minimalism: Stripped-down art that favors simple forms and few elements, like Donald Judd's boxes; the motto 'less is more' fits.
Art movements.Sonnet: A 14-line poem form that Petrarch and Shakespeare mastered; it's a poetic form, not an art movement.
Art movements.Haiku: A Japanese poem of three short lines, traditionally 5-7-5 syllables, often about nature; a poem, not an art movement.
Art movements.Fresco: Painting onto fresh, wet plaster so the pigment bonds in as it dries; Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling is the most famous example, but it's a technique.
Art movements.Sfumato: A hazy shading technique of Leonardo's, it blurs edges with soft smoke-like transitions, as in the Mona Lisa's smile.
Art movements.Chiaroscuro: Italian for 'light-dark', it is the dramatic contrast of light and shadow used by Caravaggio; a technique, not a movement.
Art movements.Easel: An artist's stand, it holds the canvas upright; the word comes from the Dutch 'ezel', meaning donkey.
Art movements.Gouache: Opaque watercolor, heavier and chalkier than regular watercolor, it dries to a matte finish; it is a paint, not a movement.
Art movements.Palette: The board a painter mixes colors on; the word also names an artist's chosen range of colors, but it's a tool, not a movement.
Art movements.Canvas: The woven cloth painters use; it spread in the Renaissance, replacing wood panels because it was lighter and cheaper to ship.
Art movements.Pastel: Soft, chalky sticks of pure pigment; Degas used them heavily for his dancers. They are a medium, not a movement.

Members of the Weasley family.Ron: The sixth of seven Weasley children, he has a famous fear of spiders and, in the books, ends up with a long Auror career.
Members of the Weasley family.Ginny: The only girl among seven siblings, she grew up playing Quidditch with her brothers and becomes a Chaser and Harry's wife.
Members of the Weasley family.Fred: With his twin, he left Hogwarts in a blaze of fireworks to open Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes; he dies in the Battle of Hogwarts.
Members of the Weasley family.George: He lost an ear to a curse during the escape from Privet Drive; with Fred, he runs the joke shop in Diagon Alley.
Members of the Weasley family.Percy: A Prefect and Head Boy, he spends years estranged from the family over his ambition at the Ministry of Magic.
