Members of the Weasley family.Charlie: The second-eldest, he works with dragons in Romania and once played Seeker at Hogwarts.
Members of the Weasley family.Arthur: The Weasley dad works at the Ministry's Misuse of Muggle Artefacts office, and loves collecting Muggle objects, like rubber ducks.
Members of the Weasley family.Molly: Famed for knitted jumpers and big dinners, she defeats Bellatrix Lestrange in the final battle with the line 'Not my daughter, you bitch!'
Members of the Weasley family.Hermione: Ron's best friend, and later his wife, but born a Granger to Muggle parents, so she isn't a Weasley by birth.
Members of the Weasley family.Neville: A Longbottom raised by his grandmother, he becomes a hero of the final battle and a Herbology professor.
Members of the Weasley family.Luna: A Ravenclaw nicknamed 'Loony', she wears radish earrings and believes in creatures like Nargles; a Lovegood.
Members of the Weasley family.Draco: A Slytherin from the Malfoy family, long a rival of Ron's family, to the point of insulting their poverty.
Members of the Weasley family.Dudley: Harry's cousin from the Dursley side, he has no relation to the Weasleys, and is unmagical.
Members of the Weasley family.Sirius: Harry's godfather, from the old Black family; he's blood-related to Tonks, not to the Weasleys.
Members of the Weasley family.Remus: A Marauder and later Defence teacher, his full name is Remus John Lupin; not related to the Weasleys.
Members of the Weasley family.Cedric: The Hufflepuff Triwizard champion, killed by Voldemort in 1995, was a Diggory, no relation.
Members of the Weasley family.Cho: A Ravenclaw Seeker, Harry's first crush, is from the Chang family, with no Weasley link.
Members of the Weasley family.Dean: A Gryffindor and a talented artist who shares a dorm with Harry and Ron, but no kin to the Weasleys.
Members of the Weasley family.Seamus: A Gryffindor from Ireland who accidentally blows things up, and Ron's dormmate, not a relative.
Members of the Weasley family.Lee Jordan: A Gryffindor and a friend of the twins who commentates Quidditch with a famous bias, not family.
Members of the Weasley family.Oliver Wood: The Gryffindor Quidditch captain who drills Harry to become Seeker, a Wood, not a Weasley.
Members of the Weasley family.Hagrid: The half-giant gamekeeper, who is Ron's friend but not a relation of the Weasleys.
Members of the Weasley family.Lavender: A Gryffindor who briefly dates Ron in the sixth book, but who is not a relative.

Sharp things.Knife: Obsidian blades from volcanic glass can be sharper than modern steel scalpels, with edges only a few nanometers thick.
Sharp things.Razor blade: A modern razor edge is ground to a width of just a few hundred atoms, and then coated to keep it from dulling after each shave.
Sharp things.Needle: Bone needles from about 50,000 years ago have been found, and the eye of the needle was among early humans' key clothing inventions.
Sharp things.Scissors: Two blades pivoting on a screw cut like a moving crossing edge, a design first used in ancient Egypt around 1500 BCE.
Sharp things.Shark tooth: Sharks can shed and replace thousands of teeth in a lifetime, with new rows rotating forward like a conveyor belt.
Sharp things.Thorn: A thorn is a modified stem, unlike a prickle on a rose, which is actually a skin outgrowth, so roses technically have prickles.
Sharp things.Broken glass: Glass breaks along curved fracture lines into edges that can be sharp at the molecular level, which is why cleaning it up needs care.
Sharp things.Axe: Stone axes were among humanity's earliest tools, and a well-honed steel head can split wood along its grain with a single swing.
Sharp things.Sword: Japanese katana blades are made by folding steel many times, building a hard edge with a flexible spine for resilience.
Sharp things.Scalpel: Surgeons' scalpels can have blades sharpened to an edge thinner than a razor, so tissue is cut with minimal tearing.
Sharp things.Thumbtack: The thumbtack is credited to Edwin Moore, who patented a push pin around 1900; its wide head lets a thumb press the sharp point in.
Sharp things.Arrowhead: Flint arrowheads were knapped by flaking off pieces, and finished ones can still cut skin after some ten thousand years.
Sharp things.Ice pick: An ice pick has a long, narrow spike for splitting ice blocks, and the same tool name later became infamous in a famous 1940 assassination.
Sharp things.Spoon: Spoons predate forks by thousands of years, and their smooth, rounded bowl is designed to hold food, not cut it.
Sharp things.Pillow: A pillow has no edges or points at all, so nothing about it can cut or pierce, and feather ones can be surprisingly dense.
Sharp things.Marble: A glass marble is smooth and rounded, and in fact it was made precisely by rolling to take away every sharp point.
Sharp things.Feather: A feather has a stiff central shaft and soft barbs that zip together with tiny hooks, and its edge cannot cut skin.
Sharp things.Butter: Butter is soft enough to spread at room temperature, and a butter knife is usually kept rounded since it doesn't need to cut.
Sharp things.Balloon: A balloon is the opposite of a sharp thing, since a sharp object is what pops it, so it's sharp's natural victim.
Sharp things.Cotton ball: Cotton fiber is a soft plant fluff from seed pods, and the fibers are so fine that a ball is mostly trapped air.
Sharp things.Crayon: A crayon is made mostly of paraffin wax with pigment, and its tip is rounded and blunt by design so children can't get hurt.
Sharp things.Eraser: Before rubber erasers, artists rubbed out pencil marks with bread crumbs, and soft rubber took over in the 1770s.
Sharp things.Sponge: Real sea sponges are simple animals with no organs, and their porous skeleton is soft and absorbent rather than sharp.
Sharp things.Rubber duck: In 1992 a container ship lost about 28,000 bath toys in the Pacific, and the drifting ducks later helped oceanographers study currents.

Things with four wheels.Car: Most cars have four wheels because it balances stability and cost, and the first self-propelled road vehicles had three.
Things with four wheels.Skateboard: Skateboards began in 1950s California as surfers' street alternative, and early ones were made from roller-skate wheels and wood.
Things with four wheels.Wagon: Wagons use front wheels that pivot, called a fifth wheel, which lets them turn in tight spaces.
Things with four wheels.Shopping cart: The shopping cart was invented in 1937 by Sylvan Goldman in Oklahoma, and shoppers at first resisted it.
Things with four wheels.Roller skate: Traditional quad roller skates have two wheels in front and two behind, unlike the in-line style.
Things with four wheels.Golf cart: Golf carts are limited to speeds around 25 kilometers per hour, and some towns allow them on certain roads.
Things with four wheels.Go-kart: Go-karts were invented in the 1950s in California, and many racing champions started in karts.
Things with four wheels.Quad bike: A quad bike has four large wheels, and its name comes from quadricycle, with all-terrain use.
Things with four wheels.Wheelchair: Wheelchairs usually have four wheels, with two large rear wheels the user can push and two small front casters.
Things with four wheels.Taxi: Most taxis are cars with four wheels, and the London black cab must have a turning circle of 25 feet.
Things with four wheels.Office chair: Most office chairs have five wheels on a star base, because five legs are more stable than four.
Things with four wheels.Bicycle: A bicycle has two wheels, and balance is kept by steering into a lean.
Things with four wheels.Tricycle: A tricycle has three wheels, and it's stable even at a standstill.
Things with four wheels.Motorcycle: Motorcycles have two wheels, and riders lean into turns to balance.
Things with four wheels.Semi truck: A typical semi truck has 18 wheels, which spread its huge load over the road.
Things with four wheels.Unicycle: A unicycle has just one wheel, and the rider balances by moving the wheel under their body.
Things with four wheels.Wheelbarrow: A wheelbarrow has one wheel, and it was invented in ancient China, probably over 2,000 years ago.
Things with four wheels.Segway: A Segway has two wheels and stays upright by using gyroscopes and motors.
Things with four wheels.Tuk-tuk: The tuk-tuk is a three-wheeled taxi, and its name imitates the sound of its small engine.
Things with four wheels.Penny-farthing: The penny-farthing has one giant front wheel and a small rear wheel, and it's named after two British coins.
Things with four wheels.Moped: A moped has two wheels and a small engine, and its name combines motor and pedal.
Things with four wheels.Hoverboard: Real hoverboards have two wheels, and they have nothing to do with the floating boards from movies.
Things with four wheels.Freight train: A freight train's cars each have many wheels in sets called trucks, and the total number runs into the hundreds.
Things with four wheels.Chariot: Ancient chariots mostly had two wheels, and light spoked wheels made them fast in battle.

Things usually thrown away after one use.Paper plate: Most paper plates get a thin plastic or clay coating so greasy food doesn't soak through, which is why many can't be recycled.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Tissue: Kleenex tissues were first marketed in the 1920s as a way to remove cold cream, and only later became the cold-season staple.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Paper napkin: Ancient Romans brought their own cloth napkin, a mappa, to dinner parties, and used it to carry leftovers home.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Diaper: A single baby can use thousands of disposable diapers before potty training, and they make up a notable slice of household landfill waste.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Paper cup: Paper cups need a thin plastic lining to hold liquid, which makes recycling them surprisingly hard.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Tea bag: Tea bags were reportedly invented by accident around 1908, when a New York merchant sent samples in silk pouches and customers brewed them whole.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Band-Aid: Band-Aids were invented in 1920 by Johnson & Johnson employee Earle Dickson, to help his accident-prone wife bandage her cuts.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Coffee filter: The paper coffee filter was invented in 1908 by German homemaker Melitta Bentz, who tore a page from her son's school notebook.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Match: Early friction matches in the 1800s used white phosphorus, which poisoned factory workers with a disfiguring jaw disease called phossy jaw.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Toothpick: Wear grooves on ancient teeth show people have picked them for ages; in the 1800s a Boston entrepreneur imported Brazilian toothpicks and promoted them.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Cotton swab: The Q-tip was invented in the 1920s, and ear doctors still advise against using swabs inside the ear canal, where they can pack wax deeper.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Postage stamp: Stamps are single-use by design: cancelling the mark stops reuse. The first, the 1840 Penny Black, was Britain's.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Party popper: Poppers fire streamers using a small charge of compressed gas or a tiny friction pellet, and the burst lasts only a moment.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Metal fork: A fork is built to be washed and reused for years; forks only became common in Europe in the Renaissance, after arriving from Italy.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Coffee mug: A mug is a keeper. Ceramic ones can last for decades, so their carbon footprint pays off after enough uses compared with paper cups.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Bath towel: Towels are reused many times between washes, and Turkish cotton towels are prized for staying absorbent and durable.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Hairbrush: Hairbrushes last for years; the first mass-produced ones came from the 1800s, and boar bristle is still used in some for spreading oils.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Dinner plate: Porcelain dinner plates are made to last generations; the material came from China, which is why we still say china for fine dishes.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Wristwatch: Wristwatches were first made for women in the 1800s; men adopted them widely after World War I, when pocket watches proved clumsy in the trenches.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Umbrella: Umbrellas are a classic reusable, though they're also among the most commonly lost items on public transport.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Frying pan: A well-seasoned cast iron frying pan can be passed down for generations, and some are still used after more than a century.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Hammer: Stone hammers are among the oldest tools, used for well over two million years, so they're far from disposable.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Pillow: Pillows date back to ancient Mesopotamia, where stone ones were used around 7,000 years ago, and are kept for years, not discarded.
Things usually thrown away after one use.Wallet: A wallet is meant to last: leather ones can age for decades, and some people carry the same one for most of their adult lives.

Things that are usually silver-colored.Aluminum foil: Kitchen foil is made from aluminum rolled paper-thin, and its shiny side and dull side perform identically when cooking.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Mercury: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and its old name, quicksilver, describes its silvery, fast-moving look.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Quarter: US quarters minted before 1965 were 90 percent silver; today's have a copper core wrapped in a silvery copper-nickel alloy.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Chrome bumper: Cars were once finished with shiny chrome bumpers in the 1950s, and today the shine is usually a thin plated layer.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Paperclip: The paperclip is made from steel wire, and Norwegians once wore it as a symbol of resistance to Nazi occupation.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Knight's armor: Plate armor was made of polished steel, and a full suit could weigh 20 to 25 kilograms, yet knights could still move and mount a horse.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Silverfish: The wingless silverfish is named for its silvery scales and fish-like wiggle, and it's an ancient insect that eats paper and glue.
Things that are usually silver-colored.DeLorean: The DeLorean DMC-12 had unpainted stainless steel body panels and starred as a time machine in Back to the Future.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Tin Man: Baum's Tin Woodman was literal tin; the 1939 film's silver look came from aluminum makeup that hospitalized the first actor cast, Buddy Ebsen.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Silver Surfer: Marvel's Silver Surfer rides a cosmic surfboard, and he began as the herald of the planet-eater Galactus.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Disco ball: A disco ball is covered with hundreds of tiny mirrors, and it scatters beams of light around a dark room into moving spots.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Stainless steel sink: Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms an invisible layer that stops rust and keeps the sink gleaming.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Oscar statuette: The Oscar is gold-plated, and it stands about 34 centimeters tall and weighs around 3.8 kilograms.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Penny: The US penny is copper-colored, though since 1982 it has mostly been zinc with a thin copper coating.
Things that are usually silver-colored.C-3PO: C-3PO is gold, not silver, and he boasts of being fluent in over six million forms of communication.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Golden Snitch: The Golden Snitch in Harry Potter is a walnut-sized ball with wings, and catching it ends a Quidditch game and earns 150 points.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Bronze medal: Bronze is mostly copper, and its brownish tone is why the bronze medal looks reddish-brown, not silvery.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Brass trumpet: Brass is a copper and zinc alloy with a yellow glow, which is why trumpets, horns, and tubas look golden.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Gold bar: A standard gold bar weighs about 12.4 kilograms, and pure gold's color is a warm, bright yellow.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Copper pipe: Copper pipe has a reddish-orange shine, and over time it turns a green patina on exposed surfaces.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Statue of Liberty: The Statue of Liberty is copper, and it's green because of oxidation; it was originally a shiny reddish brown.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Pot of gold: A pot of gold at the end of the rainbow is part of Irish folklore, guarded by a leprechaun.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Tutankhamun's mask: The famous mask of Tutankhamun is made of solid gold, weighing about 10 kilograms, inlaid with lapis lazuli and glass.
Things that are usually silver-colored.Banana: Bananas turn yellow as chlorophyll breaks down, and the Cavendish variety we eat is a clone, which leaves the crop vulnerable to disease.

Words that follow 'road'.Map: A roadmap now also means a plan for the future; the word was used that way in business long before GPS replaced paper charts.
Words that follow 'road'.Rage: Road rage became a widely used term in the late 1980s after a spate of violent motorist incidents in Los Angeles.
Words that follow 'road'.Trip: The road trip became an American institution as cars spread in the 1920s, and the Lincoln Highway was built partly for it.
Words that follow 'road'.Block: A roadblock can be a police checkpoint or any obstacle; the word also describes any hurdle blocking progress.
Words that follow 'road'.Worthy: Roadworthy means fit to be driven legally; in many countries cars must pass an annual test to prove it.
Words that follow 'road'.Works: Roadworks are repairs and construction that take up lanes; the sign for them is a person digging, used across Europe.
Words that follow 'road'.Side: Roadside bomb and roadside memorial both exist, but the original sense is simply the verge: land immediately beside the road.
Words that follow 'road'.House: A roadhouse was historically an inn along a main road for travelers, later a rowdy bar, and in 1989 a famous action movie.
Words that follow 'road'.Runner: The Road Runner is also a bird, the greater roadrunner of the US southwest, which can sprint at about 30 km/h.
Words that follow 'road'.Sign: Road signs use shapes and colors that are largely standardized across countries thanks to the 1968 Vienna Convention.
Words that follow 'road'.Test: The first driving tests became compulsory in the UK in 1935, and the original fee was just seven shillings and sixpence.
Words that follow 'road'.Lane: A trap: you hear 'lane' beside road, but 'roadlane' is not a word; lane stands alone, or follows words like fast or bus.
Words that follow 'road'.Boat: A trap: 'roadboat' isn't a word. You might think of a houseboat, or a steamboat, but not a road boat.
Words that follow 'road'.Street: Road and street are both ways, but they do not join into a compound; the word 'roadstreet' does not exist.
Words that follow 'road'.Ship: Ship attaches to many words as a suffix, like friendship, but 'roadship' isn't English, so it is a trap.
Words that follow 'road'.Plane: There is no 'roadplane' in English. An aircraft and a road are different things, even if a highway can double as a runway.
Words that follow 'road'.Light: Not a compound with road: a traffic light is two words. The first traffic light was installed outside Parliament in London in 1868.
Words that follow 'road'.Port: No 'roadport' exists. A port serves ships, though 'roadstead' is a sheltered place near the shore where ships anchor.
Words that follow 'road'.Train: A 'road train' is an Australian truck pulling several trailers, but 'roadtrain' isn't a single word players would use.
Words that follow 'road'.Ticket: Speeding tickets exist, but 'roadticket' isn't a word; you would write it as two words or just call it a traffic ticket.
Words that follow 'road'.Fare: The word 'wayfare' is related to road travel, but 'roadfare' is not a word, so this one misses.
Words that follow 'road'.Bell: No 'roadbell' exists, though bicycles have bells; the bike variant is a road bike, which is a different pairing.
Words that follow 'road'.Pump: No 'roadpump' exists; a pump with a road is just a gas station, which is usually called a filling station in the UK.
Words that follow 'road'.Fork: A fork in the road is a famous idiom, but it is a phrase of separate words rather than a compound word.

Parts inside a car engine.Piston: A piston is driven by the explosion in the cylinder, and in a typical car it moves up and down thousands of times a minute.
Parts inside a car engine.Crankshaft: The crankshaft turns the pistons' up-and-down motion into rotation, which is what finally spins the wheels.
Parts inside a car engine.Camshaft: The camshaft's lobes open and close the valves at precisely timed moments in each cycle.
Parts inside a car engine.Cylinder: Engines are often described by their cylinder count; a V8, for instance, has eight, and each is a chamber for combustion.
Parts inside a car engine.Valve: Each cylinder has at least two valves, one to let air in and one to let exhaust out, and they open thousands of times a minute.
Parts inside a car engine.Timing belt: This rubber belt synchronizes the crankshaft and camshaft, and if it snaps, some engines are badly damaged.
Parts inside a car engine.Connecting rod: This steel link joins the piston to the crankshaft, and it endures enormous forces in every rev.
Parts inside a car engine.Gasket: A head gasket seals the cylinder head and engine block, and a blown one is a famously costly repair.
Parts inside a car engine.Flywheel: A heavy flywheel stores rotational energy to smooth out the engine's power pulses.
Parts inside a car engine.Oil pump: The oil pump circulates lubricant throughout the engine, and without it, moving metal parts would seize in minutes.
Parts inside a car engine.Crankcase: The crankcase houses the crankshaft and often holds the oil reservoir below it.
Parts inside a car engine.Steering wheel: A trap: the steering wheel is in the cabin, and not inside the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Hubcap: A hubcap covers the wheel center, which is nowhere near the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Seatbelt: The modern three-point seatbelt, invented by Volvo's Nils Bohlin in 1959, is a safety feature, not an engine part.
Parts inside a car engine.Sunroof: A sunroof is a cabin feature in the roof; it doesn't belong in the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Glovebox: The glovebox is a cabin storage compartment, and has nothing to do with engine parts.
Parts inside a car engine.Wiper: Wipers clear the windshield; the intermittent wiper was invented by Robert Kearns, who spent decades suing carmakers.
Parts inside a car engine.Bumper: A bumper is on the car's outside, designed to absorb low-speed impacts, not part of the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Headlight: A headlight is on the car's front, and is not part of the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Mudflap: A mudflap hangs behind the wheels to catch spray, and sits outside the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Tailgate: The tailgate is the rear hatch; to tailgate also means to follow a car too closely.
Parts inside a car engine.Airbag: Airbags inflate in about 30 milliseconds in a crash, but they are a safety system, not an engine part.
Parts inside a car engine.Antenna: A car antenna receives radio signals, and is on the roof or the body, not inside the engine.
Parts inside a car engine.Cup holder: A cup holder is a cabin convenience, not an engine part.

Roles at a wedding.Bride: The bride is the center of the ceremony; the word is related to old Germanic terms, and white dresses became popular after Queen Victoria's 1840 wedding.
Roles at a wedding.Groom: The word groom comes from an old word for 'boy' or 'servant', and the 'bridegroom' was altered from 'bride-guma', the bride's man.
Roles at a wedding.Best man: The tradition may come from times when the best man helped the groom, and today he holds the rings and gives a speech.
Roles at a wedding.Maid of honor: The chief attendant of the bride, who helps her prepare and often gives a toast at the reception.
Roles at a wedding.Bridesmaid: Bridesmaids originated in Roman times, when attendants dressed like the bride to confuse evil spirits.
Roles at a wedding.Groomsman: Groomsmen are the groom's attendants, often a group of friends, and they help with ushering guests.
Roles at a wedding.Flower girl: A small girl scatters petals down the aisle before the bride; the custom goes back to ancient fertility rites.
Roles at a wedding.Ring bearer: A young boy carries the rings on a cushion; in practice, the rings are often fake, held by the best man.
Roles at a wedding.Officiant: The officiant, who may be a priest, a judge, or a friend ordained online, leads the ceremony and makes it legal.
Roles at a wedding.Usher: Ushers guide guests to their seats, and may be asked to seat the bride's side to the left and the groom's to the right.
Roles at a wedding.Page boy: A page boy is a young attendant who carries the bride's train, and the tradition has medieval roots in the court.
Roles at a wedding.Pallbearer: A trap: pallbearers carry the coffin at funerals, not weddings.
Roles at a wedding.Godparent: Godparents are sponsors at a christening, not at a wedding, though some are asked to serve in both.
Roles at a wedding.Valedictorian: This is the top graduate who gives a speech at graduation, not a wedding role.
Roles at a wedding.Midwife: A midwife helps with childbirth, not weddings.
Roles at a wedding.Referee: A referee enforces rules in sports, and has no role at a wedding.
Roles at a wedding.Mourner: Mourners attend funerals, which is the opposite of the happy occasion of a wedding.
Roles at a wedding.Debutante: A debutante is a young woman presented to society at a formal ball, so not a wedding role.
Roles at a wedding.Caddie: A caddie carries a golfer's clubs, and is not part of a wedding party.
Roles at a wedding.Bailiff: A bailiff is a court officer who keeps order in the courtroom, so not a wedding role.
Roles at a wedding.Cheerleader: A cheerleader leads the crowd at sports games, and has no wedding role.
Roles at a wedding.Juror: A juror decides a verdict in a trial, which is a very different kind of ceremony.
Roles at a wedding.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch over swimmers, and a lifeguard at a wedding would be a beach-wedding extra only.
Roles at a wedding.Prom king: The prom king is crowned at a school dance, and is not a wedding role.

Hair styling tools.Curling iron: In 1872, French hairdresser Marcel Grateau introduced the heated iron that made the Marcel wave.
Hair styling tools.Hair dryer: French hairdresser Alexandre Godefroy invented the first one in 1890, for use in salons.
Hair styling tools.Flat iron: The plates often exceed 200 degrees Celsius, well above boiling water, so heat protectant matters.
Hair styling tools.Crimper: Zigzag ridges squeeze hair into waves, and the look was a hit in the 1980s.
Hair styling tools.Curlers: Before curlers, people tied hair up in strips of rag overnight to get curls.
Hair styling tools.Comb: Combs found at ancient sites are more than 5,000 years old, and tooth spacing was already a design choice.
Hair styling tools.Hairbrush: Boar-bristle brushes spread the scalp's natural oils along each strand.
Hair styling tools.Diffuser: A bowl-shaped attachment spreading airflow so curls dry with less frizz.
Hair styling tools.Hair clippers: Guard numbers mark length, and in the US each number is about an eighth of an inch.
Hair styling tools.Curling wand: The clamp-free design lets you wrap hair around the barrel to form spirals, unlike a clamped iron.
Hair styling tools.Tweezers: Egyptians used bronze versions to pluck hair, so they have been grooming tools for thousands of years.
Hair styling tools.Eyelash curler: Kurlash introduced it in 1923, and it remains a rare makeup tool with little change.
Hair styling tools.Nail file: A file made of emery, a rough mineral, but it shapes nails, not hair.
Hair styling tools.Pumice stone: A volcanic rock so full of air bubbles that it floats on water, used to scrub rough skin.
Hair styling tools.Loofah: A loofah is a dried gourd, a plant, not a sea sponge, and it scrubs skin.
Hair styling tools.Toothbrush: In 15th-century China, toothbrushes had boar bristles on bone handles, and it's a hygiene tool, not styling.
Hair styling tools.Cuticle pusher: A manicure tool; some are simply sticks made from orange wood.
Hair styling tools.Mascara wand: Maybelline's name came from Mabel plus Vaseline, and its wand belongs to eye makeup.
Hair styling tools.Lint roller: Sticky sheets that peel away as you use them, and a tool for clothing, not hair.
Hair styling tools.Clothes iron: Old versions were heated on stoves, and the term sad iron meant solid iron, not unhappy.
Hair styling tools.Garment steamer: A steamer relaxes fabric wrinkles with steam and doesn't style hair.
Hair styling tools.Emery board: Emery is a rock found on the Greek island of Naxos, used as an abrasive on nail files.
Hair styling tools.Shoehorn: Helps you into a shoe without crushing the heel, and has nothing to do with hair.
Hair styling tools.Shoe brush: Cleans or polishes shoes, so it is footwear care, not hair care.

Fictional countries.Arendelle: Arendelle is the Scandinavian-style kingdom in Frozen, ruled by Elsa.

Fictional countries.Comoros: Comoros is a real island nation off East Africa, in the Indian Ocean.
Fictional countries.Palau: Palau is a real Pacific nation, with a famous jellyfish lake.
Fictional countries.Moldova: Moldova is a real country in Eastern Europe, known for huge underground wine cellars.
Fictional countries.Bhutan: Bhutan is a real country in the Himalayas, which measures 'Gross National Happiness'.

Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Hansel and Gretel: In the first edition of 1812, the mother, not a stepmother, abandons the children. Later editions softened it.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Rapunzel: The name comes from rampion, a salad herb that Rapunzel's mother craves, which leads to the whole story.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Rumpelstiltskin: A tiny man spins straw into gold for a price, and loses when the queen learns his name on the third day.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Snow White: In the Grimms' version, the queen tries three times to kill her with a lace, a comb and a poisoned apple.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.The Frog Prince: In the Grimm original, the princess throws the frog against the wall rather than kissing him.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.The Golden Goose: Anyone who touches the goose gets stuck to it, creating a silly parade that finally makes a princess laugh.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Mother Holle: A girl shakes the feather bed of Mother Holle, and the feathers fall to earth as snow.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.The Goose Girl: A princess's talking horse, Falada, keeps speaking even after he's beheaded, with his head hung on a gate.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Brave Little Tailor: The tailor boasts "seven at one blow," meaning flies, but the claim is taken as seven men.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Briar Rose: The Grimms' name for Sleeping Beauty. It's the same story as Perrault's, but with her own distinct title.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.The Little Mermaid: Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 tale, not Grimm. A statue of her sits in Copenhagen harbor.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Pinocchio: Carlo Collodi's 1883 Italian novel, about a wooden puppet whose nose grows when he lies. Not Grimm.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie's 1904 play about a boy who won't grow up. Not a Grimm tale.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Ugly Duckling: Hans Christian Andersen wrote this in 1843, so it isn't a Grimm tale.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Thumbelina: Hans Christian Andersen's tiny-girl tale from 1835, so not Grimm.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Jack & the Beanstalk: An English folk tale, best known from Joseph Jacobs's 1890 version. Not Grimm, a trap since it's a European tale.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Aladdin: An Arabian Nights story, not a Grimm tale, and added to the collection by a French translator.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Alice in Wonderland: Lewis Carroll's 1865 novel about a girl who falls down a rabbit hole. Not Grimm.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Three Little Pigs: An English folk tale, not Grimm, in which a wolf huffs and puffs at three houses.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Goldilocks: Robert Southey's English tale of 1837, in which a bear family's porridge gets sampled. Not Grimm.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.The Snow Queen: Hans Christian Andersen's 1844 tale about a girl rescuing her friend. Not Grimm.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Princess and the Pea: Hans Christian Andersen's 1835 story, so not by the Grimms.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Wizard of Oz: L. Frank Baum's 1900 American novel, not a Grimm tale.
Brothers Grimm fairy tales.Mary Poppins: P. L. Travers's 1934 novel about a magical nanny, not a Grimm tale.
